title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
summary: Gurpurab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the first Guru: his birth at Nankana Sahib, his teachings and udasis, and how Sikhs celebrate on the full moon of Katak.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, often called Guru Nanak Jayanti or simply Gurpurab, is the most widely celebrated day in the Sikh calendar. It marks the birth in 1469 of the founder of the Sikh faith, and it falls on the full moon of the month of Katak, which is why its date moves from year to year.

## Life of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji

Guru Nanak Dev Ji was born at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan, to Mehta Kalu Ji and Mata Tripta Ji. His elder sister, Bebe Nanaki Ji, was the first to recognise who he was. As a young man working at Sultanpur Lodhi he went into the river Vein and was not seen for three days; when he came out, his first words were that there is no Hindu and no Muslim, only people of the one Creator.

For more than two decades he travelled on long journeys, the udasis, with his companion Bhai Mardana Ji, reaching Assam, Sri Lanka, Tibet, Mecca and Baghdad. He taught devotion to the one Creator, honest work (kirat karni), sharing with others (vand chhakna) and remembering the Name (naam japna), and he rejected caste, empty ritual and the low status given to women. He spent his last years at Kartarpur on the Ravi, farming the land and leading the sangat in kirtan and langar.

## How Gurpurab is celebrated

Celebrations begin days earlier with Prabhat Pheris, groups singing through the streets before dawn. An Akhand Paath, a continuous reading of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, is completed on the morning of the day. Nagar Kirtans fill the streets, gurdwaras are lit, and langar is served to everyone who comes. At Nankana Sahib, sangats from across the world gather at Gurdwara Janam Asthan. Many families keep the day by rising at Amrit Vela and doing their Nitnem together.

imageCaption: Gurdwara Janam Asthan, Nankana Sahib, where Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji was born

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji, born Bhai Lehna: his service to Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the Gurmukhi script, langar at Khadur Sahib and the day today.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji celebrates the birth in 1504 of the second Sikh Guru. He was born Bhai Lehna at Matte di Sarai, near today's Sri Muktsar Sahib, to Bhai Pheru Mal and Mata Ramo (Mata Sabhirai). His life is remembered above all as an example of how far devotion and service can carry a person.

## From Bhai Lehna to Guru Angad

Bhai Lehna led groups of pilgrims each year to the shrine of the goddess Durga. On one journey he heard a Sikh reciting the bani of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, went to Kartarpur to meet the Guru, and stayed. For years he served without asking anything: carrying bundles of wet grass, working in the fields and doing whatever the Guru asked, when others turned away. Guru Nanak Dev Ji chose him as his successor over his own sons and named him Angad, a limb of his own body.

As Guru, he made Khadur Sahib the centre of the Sikh faith. He gave shape to the Gurmukhi script and taught children to read it, so that the Guru's bani could be read by ordinary people in their own language. With Mata Khivi Ji, he made langar a daily practice in which everyone sat and ate as equals. He encouraged wrestling and physical fitness among the young, and his saloks are included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Khadur Sahib and at gurdwaras everywhere for kirtan, katha and langar, and many complete an Akhand Paath. Because of his work on Gurmukhi, many families use the day to teach children to read the script, starting with the opening of Japji Sahib.
label: Prakash Purab
imageCaption: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Khadur Sahib, as published in the Mahan Kosh in 1930

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, born at Basarke: his service in old age, the langar and baoli at Goindwal Sahib, Anand Sahib, and how it is kept.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji celebrates the birth in 1479 of the third Sikh Guru, at the village of Basarke near Amritsar. He became Guru at the age of seventy-three, and his long life is remembered as proof that it is never too late to give oneself to the Guru.

## The life of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji

For many years Amar Das Ji was a devout Vaishnav who went on pilgrimage to the Ganga. Hearing Bibi Amro Ji, the daughter of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji, singing the Guru's bani, he went to Khadur Sahib and became a Sikh. Already in his sixties, he served the Guru for about twelve years, rising before dawn to carry water from the river Beas. Guru Angad Dev Ji chose him as successor.

As Guru he made Goindwal Sahib the centre of the faith. He made langar a condition of meeting him: emperor or labourer, everyone first sat in a line and ate together, a practice tradition says the emperor Akbar himself accepted. He built the baoli, a step-well of eighty-four steps, organised the growing Sikh community into twenty-two manjis for preaching, appointed women among his preachers, and spoke against sati and purdah. He composed Anand Sahib, which Sikhs recite in their Nitnem and at every Anand Karaj.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Basarke, where Gurdwara Janam Asthan marks his birthplace, and at Goindwal Sahib, where many pilgrims recite Japji Sahib on the steps of the baoli. Gurdwaras everywhere hold kirtan, Akhand Paath and langar, and the day is a natural time to reflect on serving others without ego.
label: Prakash Purab
imageCaption: Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Amar Das Ji at Basarke, near Amritsar

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji, born Bhai Jetha in Lahore: his humble service, the founding of Amritsar, the Laavan, and the celebrations in Amritsar.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji celebrates the birth in 1534 of the fourth Sikh Guru, who was born Bhai Jetha Ji in Chuna Mandi, Lahore. It is one of the most joyful days in Amritsar, the city he founded, where Sri Harmandir Sahib is lit up and the streets fill with Nagar Kirtan.

## From an orphan in Lahore to the fourth Guru

Bhai Jetha Ji lost both parents as a child and was raised by his grandmother, earning a living by selling boiled grain. He came to Goindwal Sahib with a group of pilgrims and stayed to serve Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, carrying earth and water for the building of the baoli. He married the Guru's daughter, Bibi Bhani Ji. Sikh tradition tells how the Guru asked his disciples to build platforms and then pulled them down again and again; only Bhai Jetha Ji kept rebuilding without a word of complaint. He was chosen as Guru above the Guru's own sons.

As Guru, he founded the town of Ramdaspur, later called Amritsar, and had its sarovar dug. He invited traders and craftsmen of many kinds to settle there so that the town could support itself. His bani in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji includes the Laavan, the four hymns around which the Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, is performed.

## How the day is celebrated

In Amritsar the Gurpurab is a festival for the whole city, with Nagar Kirtan, illuminations and fireworks over the sarovar. Gurdwaras everywhere hold Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, and many Sikhs make a point of visiting Sri Harmandir Sahib on or around the day.
label: Prakash Purab
imageCaption: The Amrit Sarovar at Sri Harmandir Sahib, dug at the wish of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji at Goindwal Sahib: the building of Sri Harmandir Sahib, the compiling of the Adi Granth, Sukhmani Sahib, and the day.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji celebrates the birth in 1563 of the fifth Sikh Guru at Goindwal Sahib. He was the youngest son of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji and Bibi Bhani Ji, and the grandson of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, who tradition says foresaw that the child would carry the bani across the world.

## What Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji built

Guru Arjan Dev Ji became Guru at eighteen. He completed the sarovar at Amritsar and built Sri Harmandir Sahib in its centre, setting it lower than the land around it and giving it a door on every side, as a sign that it was open to everyone. He founded the towns of Tarn Taran and Kartarpur near Jalandhar, set up a home for people with leprosy, and asked Sikhs to give dasvandh, a tenth of their earnings, for the common good.

His greatest work was the Adi Granth. With Bhai Gurdas Ji as scribe, he gathered the bani of the first four Gurus, added his own, and included the compositions of Bhagats and saints of many castes and faiths, among them Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sheikh Farid. It was installed at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604. His own bani, more than two thousand shabads, is the largest contribution to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and includes Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras hold Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, and many Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib on the day, alone or together with their sangat. His life is remembered twice in the year: on this day with joy, and in summer at his Shaheedi Purab, when Sikhs serve cold water to passers-by.
label: Prakash Purab
imageCaption: Gurdwara Bibi Bhani Ji, remembering the mother of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji at Guru Ki Wadali: Miri and Piri, the building of Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Bandi Chhor, and how the day is kept.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji celebrates the birth in 1595 of the sixth Sikh Guru at Guru Ki Wadali, a village near Amritsar. He was the only son of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Mata Ganga Ji, and his birth is remembered as an answer to his parents' long prayers, blessed by Baba Budha Ji.

## A childhood under threat

Sikh tradition remembers several attempts on the life of the young Hargobind, set in motion by his uncle Prithi Chand, who resented that the Guruship had passed to his younger brother. A nurse sent with poison and a snake in the house are among the stories told; the child came through each one. He was eleven when his father was martyred in Lahore in 1606.

## The Guru of Miri and Piri

At his Gurgaddi he wore two swords, one for Miri, worldly authority, and one for Piri, spiritual authority, and asked Sikhs to bring horses and weapons as offerings. He built Sri Akal Takht Sahib facing Sri Harmandir Sahib, raised a body of armed Sikhs, and led them in battles of defence against Mughal forces. Held for a time in the fort of Gwalior, he refused to leave unless the fifty-two kings imprisoned with him were also freed, which Sikhs remember at Bandi Chhor Divas. In his last years he founded Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej. His Guruship, about thirty-eight years, was the longest of the ten Gurus.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Gurdwara Guru Ki Wadali near Amritsar and at gurdwaras everywhere for Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar. Many gurdwaras hold katha on Miri and Piri, the balance between devotion and standing up for what is right.
label: Prakash Purab

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji, the eighth Guru and the Bal Guru: his birth at Kiratpur Sahib, his care for the sick in Delhi, and the day.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji celebrates the birth in 1656 of the eighth Sikh Guru at Kiratpur Sahib, to Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji and Mata Kishan Kaur Ji. He became Guru at the age of five and is remembered with deep affection as the Bal Guru, the child Guru.

## The child who became Guru

Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji passed over his elder son, Ram Rai, who had altered a line of the Guru's bani to please the emperor Aurangzeb, and entrusted the Guruship to his younger son. Despite his age, Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji was known for his calm wisdom and composure. Sikh tradition tells of a proud pandit at Panjokhra who challenged the young Guru to explain the Gita; the Guru asked a passing water-carrier, Chhajju, to answer instead, and the unlettered man spoke with such insight that the pandit was humbled.

Summoned to Delhi by the emperor, the Guru stayed at the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh of Amber. When smallpox and cholera spread through the city, he served the sick of every faith and gave them water from the well there. He caught smallpox himself and passed away in 1664, aged about eight, after indicating that the next Guru would be found at Bakala. The bungalow is now Gurdwara Bangla Sahib.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark the day with Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, especially at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib and Gurdwara Bala Sahib in Delhi. Many take home water from the sarovar at Bangla Sahib, and Sikhs everywhere remember him at the close of every Ardas, which asks that the sorrows of all who remember him be taken away.
label: Prakash Purab
imageCaption: The sarovar at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, Delhi

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji in Amritsar: how Tyag Mal became Tegh Bahadur, his years at Bakala, his bani, and how the day is observed.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji celebrates the birth in 1621 of the ninth Sikh Guru at Guru Ke Mahal in Amritsar. He was the youngest son of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji and Mata Nanaki Ji, and was named Tyag Mal, master of renunciation, a name that fitted his quiet, inward nature.

## Brave of the sword

Tyag Mal grew up among the Sikhs who trained in arms under his father, and at about thirteen he fought beside him in the battle of Kartarpur against a Mughal force. His courage there earned him the name Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword. He married Mata Gujri Ji, and after his father's passing he lived for many years at Bakala, spending long hours in meditation.

## The Guru

When Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji said only that the next Guru was at Bakala, many claimants appeared there. The trader Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana recognised the true Guru in the meditating Tegh Bahadur Ji, and climbed onto a roof to announce it. As Guru he travelled widely through Punjab, to the east as far as Assam, and to Patna, where his son, the future Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, was born. He founded Chakk Nanaki, which grew into Anandpur Sahib. His shabads and saloks, included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, are treasured for their call to steadiness, fearlessness and detachment. In 1675 he gave his life in Delhi for the freedom of others to follow their faith.

## How the day is observed

The day is marked with Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, especially at Gurdwara Guru Ke Mahal in Amritsar and at Baba Bakala Sahib. Many Sikhs recite his saloks, which close the reading of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at a Sahaj or Akhand Paath.
label: Prakash Purab

title: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
summary: The Gurpurab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, born Gobind Rai at Patna Sahib: his childhood, the Khalsa, his writing and sacrifice, and how Sikhs celebrate the day.
body:
The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji celebrates the birth in 1666 of the tenth Sikh Guru. He was born Gobind Rai at Patna, in Bihar, to Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji and Mata Gujri Ji, while his father was travelling in the east. Takht Sri Harimandir Ji, Patna Sahib, one of the five Takhts, marks the place.

## Childhood and Guruship

Gobind Rai spent his early years in Patna, where tradition remembers his games with the local children and the love of the townspeople, before the family moved to Anandpur Sahib. In 1675 Kashmiri Pandits came to his father seeking protection from forced conversion; the nine-year-old is remembered as saying that no one was more worthy to stand for them than his father. After Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji gave his life in Delhi, Gobind Rai became Guru.

## Saint, soldier and poet

At Anandpur Sahib and Paonta Sahib he trained in arms, studied languages and gathered poets and scholars around him. On Vaisakhi in 1699 he created the Khalsa, giving the Sikhs Amrit, the five Ks and the name Singh or Kaur. He fought many battles in defence and lost his father, his mother and all four of his sons, yet remained without bitterness. Before his Joti Jot at Nanded in 1708 he passed the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Guru Khalsa Panth.

## How the day is celebrated

The Gurpurab is celebrated with Akhand Paath, Prabhat Pheris, Nagar Kirtan and langar, above all at Patna Sahib, where sangats come from across the world. Gurdwaras everywhere hold kirtan of his compositions, and many Sikhs read Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Savaiye, his banis in the Nitnem.
label: Prakash Purab
imageCaption: Takht Sri Harimandir Ji, Patna Sahib, the birthplace of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji

title: First Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (1604)
summary: The first installation of the Adi Granth at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604: how Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled it, who wrote it out, and how the Pehla Prakash is kept.
body:
The Pehla Prakash Purab remembers the day in 1604 when the Adi Granth, the scripture that became Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, was installed for the first time in Sri Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. It is one of the most joyful days at Sri Harmandir Sahib, which is lit and decorated for the occasion.

## How the Adi Granth was compiled

Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji gathered the bani of the first four Gurus, much of it kept in pothis held by the families of earlier Gurus, and added his own. He also included the compositions of Bhagats and saints from many castes, regions and faiths, among them Bhagat Kabir Ji, Bhagat Ravidas Ji, Bhagat Namdev Ji and Sheikh Farid Ji, so that the scripture spoke for all of humanity rather than one community. The work was done beside the pool at Ramsar in Amritsar, with Bhai Gurdas Ji as the scribe, and it was arranged by raag, the musical measures in which the bani is sung.

## The first Prakash

When the Granth was complete it was carried in procession to Sri Harmandir Sahib. Tradition remembers that Baba Budha Ji carried it on his head while the Guru walked behind with a chaur, and that Baba Budha Ji was appointed the first granthi. The Guru gave the scripture the place of honour and sat below it. A century later, in 1708, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji conferred the Guruship on it, completed with the bani of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji.

## How the day is observed

Sangats hold Akhand Paath, kirtan and Nagar Kirtan, and Sri Harmandir Sahib is illuminated. Many gurdwaras hold katha about the compiling of the Granth, and it is a fitting day to begin a Sahaj Paath at home.
label: Prakash Purab
imageCaption: Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, where the Adi Granth was first installed in 1604

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji
summary: How Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji chose Bhai Lehna as his successor at Kartarpur and named him Angad, passing over his own sons, and how the Gurgaddi Purab is observed.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji remembers the day in 1539 when Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji passed the Guruship to his devoted Sikh, Bhai Lehna Ji, at Kartarpur on the banks of the Ravi. It set the principle that would guide every succession after it: the Guruship goes by devotion and service, not by birth.

## The tests of Bhai Lehna

Bhai Lehna Ji had come to Kartarpur as a devotee of the goddess Durga and stayed to serve. Sikh tradition remembers the tests Guru Nanak Dev Ji set for his followers. He asked them to carry bundles of wet grass dripping with mud, which spoiled Bhai Lehna's fine clothes; he asked them to pull a bowl from a muddy drain on a winter night; and once he walked into a forest strewn with coins and then with jewels, and one by one his followers stopped to pick them up. Only Bhai Lehna Ji kept following, obeying each instruction without question. The Guru's own sons, Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das, did not.

## The Guruship passes

Guru Nanak Dev Ji placed a coconut and five paise before Bhai Lehna Ji, bowed to him, and asked Baba Budha Ji to apply the tilak of Guruship. He named him Angad, from ang, a limb of his own body, saying that the light was the same and only the body had changed. Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji then moved to Khadur Sahib to carry the Guru's work forward, where he shaped the Gurmukhi script and spread the langar.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas at Khadur Sahib, at Kartarpur Sahib in Pakistan and in gurdwaras everywhere. Katha on the day often dwells on humility and obedience as the qualities the Guru looks for.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, where Bhai Lehna Ji received the Guruship

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Sahib Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
summary: How Sri Guru Amar Das Ji became the third Guru at Khadur Sahib after twelve years of service in old age, the story of the weaver's hut, and how the day is kept.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji remembers the day in 1552 when Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji entrusted the Guruship to him at Khadur Sahib. He was seventy-three, and had spent about twelve years in humble service to the Guru. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps this anniversary on a fixed solar date.

## Twelve years of seva

Every day before dawn, Amar Das Ji walked to the river Beas at Goindwal, filled a pitcher and carried it back for the Guru's bath, reciting the bani on the way. Sikh tradition tells of a stormy winter night when, returning in the dark, he stumbled against a weaver's loom near a hut. The weaver's wife called out that it could only be Amru, the homeless old man. When the story reached Guru Angad Dev Ji, he embraced his servant and called him the home of the homeless, the honour of those without honour, the strength of those without strength.

## The Guruship

Guru Angad Dev Ji's son Datu resented being passed over and, tradition says, kicked the new Guru from his seat. Guru Amar Das Ji is remembered as asking whether his old bones had hurt Datu's foot, and quietly left for his native Basarke until the Sikhs found him. He went on to make Goindwal Sahib the centre of the faith, build its baoli, organise the sangats into manjis and make the langar a practice of equality.

## How the day is observed

The day is marked with kirtan and Ardas at Khadur Sahib and Goindwal Sahib, and in gurdwaras everywhere. It is a day when katha returns to the theme of his life: that patience and service, at any age, are what the Guru honours.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Gurdwara Sri Khadur Sahib in the 1920s, from the first edition of the Mahan Kosh

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
summary: How Bhai Jetha Ji, the son-in-law of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, was chosen as the fourth Guru at Goindwal Sahib, the test of the platforms, and how the day is observed.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji remembers the day in 1574 when Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, at Goindwal Sahib, entrusted the Guruship to Bhai Jetha Ji, who became the fourth Sikh Guru. Like each Guru before him, he was chosen for his devotion rather than his family.

## The test of the platforms

Bhai Jetha Ji had served at Goindwal for years, carrying baskets of earth for the baoli and serving in the langar, and had married the Guru's daughter, Bibi Bhani Ji. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Amar Das Ji asked his two sons-in-law, Bhai Rama Ji and Bhai Jetha Ji, to build platforms by the river. Each time they finished, the Guru found fault and asked that they be pulled down and built again. Bhai Rama Ji eventually gave up, saying he had done exactly what was asked. Bhai Jetha Ji kept rebuilding, asking forgiveness for his own lack of understanding, until the Guru embraced him.

## The fourth Guru

Guru Amar Das Ji gave him the name Ram Das, servant of God, and asked Baba Budha Ji to apply the tilak of Guruship. Sri Guru Ram Das Ji went on to found the town of Ramdaspur, now Amritsar, dig the sarovar around which Sri Harmandir Sahib would rise, and compose the Laavan of the Anand Karaj. Before his own passing he chose his youngest son, Arjan Dev Ji, beginning a line of Gurus from the Sodhi family.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas at Goindwal Sahib, at Amritsar and in gurdwaras everywhere. Katha often returns to the platforms: the Guru's work is done with humility, not by insisting one is right.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: The Baoli Sahib at Goindwal, where Bhai Jetha Ji served Sri Guru Amar Das Ji

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
summary: How Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji became the fifth Guru at Goindwal Sahib, the letters of longing he sent his father from Lahore, Prithi Chand's opposition, and the day.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji remembers the day in 1581 when Sri Guru Ram Das Ji entrusted the Guruship to his youngest son at Goindwal Sahib, shortly before his own Joti Jot. Arjan Dev Ji was eighteen.

## The letters from Lahore

Sikh tradition tells that Guru Ram Das Ji sent Arjan Dev Ji to Lahore to attend a family wedding and asked him to stay until called. Separated from his father for a long time, the young man wrote letters full of longing to see him. The first two were intercepted by his eldest brother, Prithi Chand, who kept them hidden. When the third letter reached the Guru, he called his son home and asked about the first two, and Prithi Chand's deceit came to light. These letters of longing are remembered as the Shabad Hazare, and many Sikhs recite them each day.

## A Guruship met with patience

Prithi Chand never accepted the decision and worked against his younger brother for years, setting up a rival seat and trying to cut off the offerings of the sangat. Guru Arjan Dev Ji answered with patience. Over the next quarter of a century he completed Sri Harmandir Sahib, founded Tarn Taran and Kartarpur, compiled the Adi Granth in 1604 and gave the Sikhs a strong, organised community. In 1606 he became the first Sikh Guru to be martyred.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras mark the day with kirtan and Ardas, and many Sikhs recite the Shabad Hazare and Sukhmani Sahib. Sangats gather at Goindwal Sahib, where the Guruship passed, and at Sri Harmandir Sahib.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Sri Harmandir Sahib, completed by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
summary: How Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji became the sixth Guru after the shaheedi of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, wore the swords of Miri and Piri, and built Sri Akal Takht Sahib.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1606 when he became the sixth Sikh Guru, still a boy of eleven, after the shaheedi of his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, in Lahore. His Guruship changed the shape of the Sikh community.

## Miri and Piri

Before his martyrdom, Guru Arjan Dev Ji is remembered as sending word that his son should sit on the throne fully armed and keep an army as far as he could. At the ceremony, Baba Budha Ji brought the seli, the woollen cord worn by the earlier Gurus. Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji asked that it be placed in the treasury and instead wore two swords: one of Miri, worldly authority, and one of Piri, spiritual authority. He explained that the seli would now be worn as a sword belt, and asked Sikhs to bring horses and weapons as offerings.

## The Akal Takht

Facing Sri Harmandir Sahib he built a raised platform, the Akal Bunga, now Sri Akal Takht Sahib, the Throne of the Timeless. There he held court, heard the sangat's disputes, watched wrestling and martial exercises and listened to ballads of heroism, while Sri Harmandir Sahib remained the place of the Word. The pairing of the two buildings is itself a picture of Miri and Piri: devotion and the duty to stand up for justice, side by side.

## How the day is observed

The day is observed with kirtan, Akhand Paath and Ardas, especially at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. Many gurdwaras hold katha on the meaning of Miri and Piri, and some hold displays of gatka, the Sikh martial art.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Sri Akal Takht Sahib and Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
summary: How Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji chose his grandson Har Rai Ji as the seventh Guru at Kiratpur Sahib, the story of the flower, and how the Gurgaddi Purab is kept.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1644 when Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, at Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej, entrusted the Guruship to his grandson. Har Rai Ji, the son of Baba Gurditta Ji and Mata Nihal Kaur Ji, was fourteen. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps the anniversary on a fixed solar date.

## The flower and the robe

Sikh tradition tells that as a boy, Har Rai Ji was walking in a garden when his long robe caught a rose bush and some petals fell. He stopped, saddened. His grandfather is remembered as telling him that a robe should be gathered in so that it harms nothing as one passes; and Har Rai Ji carried that lesson for the rest of his life. He is remembered as the gentlest of the Gurus, with a deep love of nature and every living thing.

## A peaceful Guruship

Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji passed over his own surviving sons and chose the boy for his devotion and character. As Guru, Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji kept a body of about two thousand mounted Sikhs, as his grandfather had asked, but his years were largely peaceful and given to preaching in Punjab, the Malwa and beyond. He kept gardens and a dispensary of herbal medicines at Kiratpur Sahib, and tradition remembers that he sent medicine that healed Dara Shikoh, the son of the emperor Shah Jahan, without regard to the family's past hostility.

## How the day is observed

The day is marked with kirtan and Ardas at Kiratpur Sahib and in gurdwaras everywhere. Katha often turns to his care for living things, and some sangats plant trees in his memory.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Kiratpur Sahib, where Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji received the Guruship

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
summary: Why Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji passed over his elder son Ram Rai and entrusted the Guruship to five-year-old Harkrishan Ji at Kiratpur Sahib, and how the day is kept.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1661 when Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji, shortly before his Joti Jot at Kiratpur Sahib, entrusted the Guruship to his younger son, then about five years old. Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji became the eighth Guru and the youngest.

## Why Ram Rai was passed over

Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji had sent his elder son, Ram Rai, to the court of the emperor Aurangzeb in Delhi to answer questions about the Guru's bani. Ram Rai impressed the court with miracles, and when asked about a line of Guru Nanak Dev Ji's bani that the emperor's advisers said insulted Muslims, he changed a word to please them. When this reached the Guru, he refused ever to see Ram Rai again, saying that the Guru's bani could not be altered for anyone. The Guruship went instead to the child whose devotion and composure the Guru trusted.

## The Bal Guru

Ram Rai disputed the succession and asked Aurangzeb to intervene, which is why the young Guru was later summoned to Delhi. There Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji served the sick through an epidemic of smallpox and cholera before falling ill himself. His Guruship lasted under three years, yet he is remembered in every Ardas, which asks that the sorrows of all who remember him be taken away. Ram Rai later settled in the hills, where the town of Dehradun grew around his dera.

## How the day is observed

The day is marked with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Kiratpur Sahib and at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi. It is often a day when children take part in the kirtan and the Ardas.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej, where the Guruship passed to Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji
summary: How the ninth Guru was found at Baba Bakala among twenty-two claimants: the vow of Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana, the cry of Guru ladho re, and how the day is observed.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji remembers how the ninth Guru was recognised at Bakala, a town near Amritsar, in 1664. Before his Joti Jot in Delhi, Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji had said only two words about his successor: Baba Bakale, the Baba is at Bakala.

## Twenty-two claimants

Bakala was home to Tegh Bahadur Ji, the youngest son of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, who had lived there for many years in quiet meditation. But as word spread, twenty-two members of the Sodhi family set themselves up there as Guru, each with a following and a seat, among them Dhir Mal, who held the original pothi of the Adi Granth. The sangat did not know which to follow.

## Guru ladho re

Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana was a trader whose ship had been caught in a storm. He had prayed to the Guru and vowed an offering of five hundred gold coins if he came safely to shore. Arriving at Bakala and finding so many Gurus, he placed two coins before each claimant, knowing that the true Guru would ask for what was promised. None did, until he was led to Tegh Bahadur Ji, who asked why he was giving two when he had vowed five hundred, and showed the mark on his shoulder where he had pushed the ship to safety. Makhan Shah climbed onto a roof and called to the sangat: Guru ladho re, I have found the Guru.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan, katha and Ardas, above all at Baba Bakala Sahib, which holds a large Jorh Mela, Rakhar Puniya, every summer to remember the day.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Baba Bakala, where the ninth Guru was recognised

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
summary: How Gobind Rai became the tenth Guru at Anandpur Sahib at the age of nine after the shaheedi of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, and how the Gurgaddi Purab is kept.
body:
The Gurgaddi Purab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji remembers the day in 1675 when Gobind Rai, nine years old, became the tenth Sikh Guru at Anandpur Sahib, after his father, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, gave his life in Delhi.

## A child's answer

Earlier that year a group of Kashmiri Pandits, led by Pandit Kirpa Ram of Mattan, came to Anandpur Sahib. They were being pressed to convert under the emperor Aurangzeb and asked the Guru for help. Sikh tradition remembers the Guru sitting deep in thought and saying that only the sacrifice of a great soul could turn the tide. The young Gobind Rai, coming in, asked who could be greater than his father to make that sacrifice. Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji told the Pandits to inform the emperor that if he could convert the Guru, they would all follow.

## The Guruship

Before leaving for Delhi, Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji named his son as his successor. After the shaheedi at Chandni Chowk, Bhai Jaita Ji carried the Guru's head to Anandpur Sahib, where the young Guru received it with honour and declared that his followers would never again be hard to recognise. Over the next thirty-three years Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji trained the Sikhs in arms and letters, created the Khalsa in 1699, wrote a large body of bani and poetry, and at the end passed the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Guru Khalsa Panth.

## How the day is observed

The day is marked with kirtan, katha and Ardas, especially at Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib in Anandpur Sahib. Katha on the day often tells of the courage of the child who sent his father to stand for the faith of others.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur Sahib, in about 1952

title: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (Nanded, 1708)
summary: In 1708 at Nanded, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji ended the line of human Gurus and gave the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. The story and how Gurta Gaddi Divas is kept.
body:
Gurta Gaddi Divas remembers the day in 1708 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, at Nanded on the banks of the Godavari, ended the line of human Gurus and conferred the Guruship on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Since that day Sikhs have bowed to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji as their living Guru, the Guru present in the Word.

## The Damdami Bir

The Adi Granth compiled by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji in 1604 did not yet hold the bani of the ninth Guru. At Damdama Sahib, Talwandi Sabo, in 1706, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji had the whole scripture written out again, adding the shabads and saloks of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, with Bhai Mani Singh Ji as the scribe. This version, the Damdami Bir, is the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji Sikhs read today, its 1430 angs holding the bani of six Gurus and of Bhagats and saints of many backgrounds.

## The Guruship passes to the Word

Wounded by an assassin at Nanded and knowing his time was near, the Guru gathered the sangat. Tradition remembers that he placed five paise and a coconut before the Granth, bowed to it, and declared that from then on Sikhs should regard it as their Guru, with the Guru Khalsa Panth, the community acting together, guided by it. No living person would hold the Guruship again. Sikhs recall the instruction in the Dohra sung after Ardas.

## How the day is observed

The day is celebrated with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Nagar Kirtan, above all at Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib in Nanded, which held a great celebration at the tercentenary in 2008. In homes and gurdwaras, it is a day to give thanks for the Guru who is always present and always within reach.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, Nanded

title: Guruship conferred to Panj Pyare / Guru Khalsa at Chamkaur Sahib
summary: At the garhi of Chamkaur Sahib, five Singhs acting as the Panj Pyare asked Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji to leave, and the Guru obeyed the Khalsa. The story of the day.
body:
This day remembers a turning point at Chamkaur Sahib in December 1704, when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji accepted an instruction from the Khalsa itself. Five Singhs, standing as the Panj Pyare, asked the Guru to leave the besieged fortress so that he could live to lead the Panth, and the Guru obeyed, honouring the Khalsa as his own form.

## The garhi at Chamkaur

After leaving Anandpur Sahib and losing much of the sangat at the flooded Sirsa river, the Guru reached Chamkaur with his two elder sons and about forty Singhs. They took shelter in a mud fortress, a garhi, and were surrounded by a far larger Mughal army. Through the day the Singhs went out in small groups to fight, and both elder Sahibzade, Baba Ajit Singh Ji and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, gave their lives.

## The Khalsa decides

By nightfall only a handful of Singhs were left. They urged the Guru to escape, and when he refused, five of them stood together as the Panj Pyare and gave the instruction as the Khalsa. Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, who had himself taken Amrit from the first Panj Pyare in 1699, accepted. Tradition remembers that he placed his kalgi and dress on Bhai Sangat Singh Ji, who resembled him, and declared that the Guru lives in the Khalsa. He left under cover of darkness with Bhai Daya Singh Ji, Bhai Dharam Singh Ji and Bhai Man Singh Ji, clapping and calling out as he went. The Singhs who stayed fought on until they fell.

## How the day is remembered

The day is remembered as the time the Guru placed his authority in the Guru Khalsa, the five acting together, a principle that still guides Panthic decisions. Gurdwaras at Chamkaur Sahib hold kirtan, katha and Ardas during the Shaheedi Jorh Mela.
label: Gurgaddi
imageCaption: Gurdwara Garhi Sahib, Chamkaur Sahib, on the site of the mud fortress

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
summary: How Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, passed the Guruship to Guru Angad Dev Ji and merged with the Divine Light in 1539, and the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji remembers the day in 1539 when the founder of the Sikh faith completed his life on earth at Kartarpur, on the right bank of the Ravi, and merged with the Divine Light. Sikhs speak of the passing of a Guru as joti jot, light merging into light.

## Kartarpur, the town of the Creator

After more than twenty years of travelling on his udasis, Guru Nanak Dev Ji settled at Kartarpur, a town he founded, and spent about eighteen years there. He took off the dress of a traveller and worked the fields himself, showing that a spiritual life is lived in the middle of ordinary work and family. The day began before dawn with Japji Sahib and kirtan, and closed with Sodar and Arti; in between, everyone who came ate together in the langar. Here Bhai Lehna Ji served him and was chosen as Guru Angad.

## The sheet of flowers

Sikh tradition remembers that as the Guru's end drew near, his Hindu followers wished to cremate him and his Muslim followers to bury him. The Guru asked each group to place flowers on either side of him, and said that those whose flowers were still fresh in the morning could perform the rites. In the morning both sets of flowers were fresh, and when the sheet was lifted the body was gone. The sheet was divided, and today a samadh and a grave stand side by side at Kartarpur.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember the day with kirtan, katha and Ardas in Punjab and around the world. Since the Kartarpur Corridor opened in 2019, pilgrims from India can visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, without a visa, and many make the journey on or near this day.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, where Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his last years

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
summary: Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji completed his life at Khadur Sahib in 1552 after passing the Guruship to Sri Guru Amar Das Ji. His work for Gurmukhi and langar, and the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji remembers the day in 1552 when the second Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Khadur Sahib, near the river Beas, having entrusted the Guruship to Sri Guru Amar Das Ji. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps the anniversary on a fixed solar date.

## What he left the Sikhs

In about thirteen years as Guru, Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji gave the young community much of its early shape. He developed and spread the Gurmukhi script, so that the bani could be written and read by ordinary people, and opened schools where children learned to read it. He gathered the hymns of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, and tradition credits him with collecting the accounts of the first Guru's life that grew into the Janamsakhis. He encouraged wrestling and physical fitness, and kept an akhara at Khadur Sahib for the young men of the village.

Mata Khivi Ji, his wife, ran the langar at Khadur Sahib, where everyone who came was fed, and she is the only woman named in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, in a Vaar by Bhai Satta and Bhai Balvand that praises the rich kheer of her kitchen. Under her care the langar became a daily feature of Sikh life.

## Choosing his successor

Like Guru Nanak Dev Ji before him, Guru Angad Dev Ji passed over his own sons, Dasu and Datu, and chose the elderly Amar Das Ji, who had served him for twelve years.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas at Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Khadur Sahib, and in gurdwaras everywhere, to remember his life of service.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: A Sikh congregation at a katha in Tarn Taran district, around 1900

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Ji / Goindwal Sahib Jorh Mela
summary: Sri Guru Amar Das Ji completed his life at Goindwal Sahib in 1574, aged ninety-five. His work, the baoli of eighty-four steps, and the Jorh Mela held there on the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji remembers the day in 1574 when the third Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Goindwal Sahib, at the age of about ninety-five, having entrusted the Guruship to Sri Guru Ram Das Ji. The day is marked by a Jorh Mela at Goindwal Sahib.

## Twenty-two years as Guru

Sri Guru Amar Das Ji became Guru in his seventies and led the Sikhs for about twenty-two years. He made Goindwal Sahib the centre of the faith and built its baoli, a step-well reached by eighty-four steps. He made langar a condition of meeting him, so that rich and poor, high caste and low, sat in one line and ate the same food. He divided the growing community into twenty-two manjis, appointed preachers among them women, spoke against sati and purdah, and set Vaisakhi, Diwali and Maghi as days when Sikhs gathered at Goindwal. He composed Anand Sahib, sung at the close of every Sikh service and at every Anand Karaj.

## The passing of the Guruship

Before his passing he chose his son-in-law, Bhai Jetha Ji, over his own sons, and asked the family and the sangat to bow to him as Guru Ram Das. Tradition remembers that he asked that no one weep for him, but that kirtan be sung instead.

## The Jorh Mela at Goindwal

Pilgrims come to Goindwal Sahib in large numbers for the Jorh Mela. Many walk down the eighty-four steps of the baoli and recite Japji Sahib once on each step, a practice tradition links to freedom from the cycle of eighty-four lakh births, and bathe in its water. Gurdwaras everywhere hold kirtan and Ardas.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, Goindwal, built by Sri Guru Amar Das Ji

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
summary: Sri Guru Ram Das Ji completed his life at Goindwal Sahib in 1581 after naming Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji as Guru. The city he founded, the Laavan, and the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji remembers the day in 1581 when the fourth Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Goindwal Sahib, after entrusting the Guruship to his youngest son, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji. He was forty-seven, and had been Guru for about seven years.

## A city and a sarovar

In those seven years Sri Guru Ram Das Ji founded the town first called Guru Ka Chakk and then Ramdaspur, which grew into Amritsar. He had the sarovar dug, the pool of nectar that gave the city its name, around which his son would raise Sri Harmandir Sahib. He invited traders and craftsmen of fifty-two trades to settle there, and the bazaar he founded, Guru Bazaar, still stands. He appointed masands to look after distant sangats and collect their offerings for the Guru's work.

## His bani

His bani in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is sung in thirty raags and is known for its tenderness and longing. It includes the Laavan, the four hymns around which the couple walk at an Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, and a number of the shabads Sikhs recite in Rehras Sahib and Sohila Sahib each evening.

## Choosing Guru Arjan Dev Ji

His eldest son, Prithi Chand, wanted the Guruship and resented the choice; his second son, Mahadev, had turned to an ascetic life. The Guru chose Arjan Dev Ji, whose letters of longing from Lahore had shown his devotion, and asked Baba Budha Ji to perform the ceremony before the sangat.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember him with kirtan, katha and Ardas at Goindwal Sahib, at Amritsar and in gurdwaras everywhere.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, Goindwal, around 1900

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
summary: Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji completed his life at Kiratpur Sahib in 1644 after the longest Guruship of the ten Gurus. Patalpuri Sahib, his legacy, and the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1644 when the sixth Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Kiratpur Sahib, on the banks of the Sutlej. His Guruship of about thirty-eight years was the longest of the ten Gurus. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps the anniversary on a fixed solar date.

## A Guruship of Miri and Piri

Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji became Guru as a boy after the shaheedi of his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, and changed the course of Sikh history. He wore two swords for Miri and Piri, built Sri Akal Takht Sahib, raised a body of armed Sikhs and fought four battles of defence against Mughal forces. Imprisoned at Gwalior, he secured the release of fifty-two kings along with his own, which Sikhs remember at Bandi Chhor Divas. He also travelled to preach, as far as Kashmir and Pilibhit.

## Kiratpur Sahib

In his last decade he settled at Kiratpur Sahib, a town founded on land given by the Raja of Kahlur, and lived there in relative peace. His eldest son, Baba Gurditta Ji, passed away before him, and the Guru chose Baba Gurditta's younger son, Har Rai Ji, as his successor, recognising his gentleness and devotion. Before his passing he asked his followers to accept the boy as Guru.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib at Kiratpur, where his last rites took place on the bank of the Sutlej, is visited by many on the day; it is also where many Sikh families bring the ashes of their loved ones. Sangats hold kirtan and Ardas there and in gurdwaras everywhere.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib, Kiratpur, where the last rites of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji took place

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji
summary: Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji completed his life at Kiratpur Sahib in 1661 after naming his young son Harkrishan Ji as Guru. His love of nature, his healing and the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1661 when the seventh Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Kiratpur Sahib, aged about thirty-one, after entrusting the Guruship to his younger son, Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji.

## The gentlest of the Gurus

Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji was the grandson of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji and is remembered for his tenderness towards every living thing. He kept gardens and a small zoo at Kiratpur Sahib, and a dispensary of herbal medicines open to anyone in need. Sikh tradition tells that when Dara Shikoh, the eldest son of the emperor Shah Jahan, fell gravely ill and the court physicians could do nothing, the Guru sent the herbs that healed him, saying that a tree gives shade even to the one who cuts it.

## A Guruship of preaching

He kept a body of about two thousand mounted Sikhs, as his grandfather had wished, but his years as Guru were largely peaceful. He travelled through the Malwa and the Doaba, and sent preachers further afield; among those he blessed was Phul, from whom the ruling families of Patiala, Nabha and Jind later descended.

## The succession

Summoned to the court of the emperor Aurangzeb, the Guru sent his elder son Ram Rai instead. When Ram Rai altered a line of the Guru's bani to please the court, the Guru disowned him and chose his younger son, Harkrishan Ji, then five, as the eighth Guru.

## How the day is observed

Sikhs remember him with kirtan and Ardas at Kiratpur Sahib and in gurdwaras everywhere, and katha often turns to his compassion and his care for nature.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: Gurdwara Charan Kamal, Kiratpur Sahib

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
summary: The eighth Guru served the sick of Delhi through an epidemic and passed away in 1664, aged about eight, after naming Baba Bakale. Bangla Sahib, Bala Sahib and the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1664 when the eighth Sikh Guru, still a child of about eight, completed his life on earth in Delhi. Sikhs remember him as the Bal Guru, and for the compassion he showed the sick in his last days.

## Called to Delhi

His elder brother, Ram Rai, disputed his Guruship and asked the emperor Aurangzeb to intervene, and the young Guru was summoned to Delhi. Raja Jai Singh of Amber, a noble at the court, offered him his bungalow in the city, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib now stands. Tradition remembers that the Guru never met the emperor, and that the Raja's queen, testing him, dressed as a maid among her attendants, and the child walked past the others to sit in her lap.

## Serving the sick

That year smallpox and cholera spread through Delhi. The Guru went among the sick of every faith, comforting them and giving them water from the well at the bungalow, and many recovered. He caught smallpox himself. As he lay ill, the sangat asked who would lead them after him. He asked for five paise and a coconut, moved them in a circle, and said only Baba Bakale, the Baba is at Bakala, pointing to his great-uncle, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji.

## How the day is observed

His last rites took place on the bank of the Yamuna, where Gurdwara Bala Sahib now stands. Sangats gather for kirtan, katha and Ardas at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib and Gurdwara Bala Sahib, many praying for those who are ill, and take home water from the sarovar at Bangla Sahib.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, Delhi, the bungalow where Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji stayed

title: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
summary: Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji completed his life at Nanded in 1708 after passing the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Khalsa. His last year and the day.
body:
The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji remembers the day in October 1708 when the tenth Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Nanded, on the banks of the Godavari in the Deccan, some weeks after he was wounded by an assassin. Before his passing he gave the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Guru Khalsa Panth.

## The road to Nanded

In the years before, the Guru had lost his father, his mother and all four of his sons, and had left Anandpur Sahib. After the death of the emperor Aurangzeb in 1707, his successor Bahadur Shah invited the Guru to meet him, and the Guru travelled south with the emperor's camp. At Nanded he met an ascetic, Madho Das Bairagi, who became his Sikh, took the name Banda Singh, and was sent to Punjab to lead the Khalsa.

## The last days

Two Pathans, believed to have been sent by Wazir Khan of Sirhind, came to the Guru's camp, and one stabbed him. The wound was stitched and began to heal, but it opened again when the Guru drew a heavy bow. Knowing his time had come, he gathered the sangat, placed five paise and a coconut before Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, bowed to it, and told the Sikhs that the Granth was now their Guru and the Khalsa its body. Tradition remembers his last instructions as asking the Sikhs to sing kirtan rather than mourn.

## How the day is observed

Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, one of the five Takhts, stands at the place. Sangats gather there and in gurdwaras around the world for kirtan, katha and Ardas, remembering a life given wholly to the Panth.
label: Joti Jot
imageCaption: Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, Nanded, where Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji completed his life

title: Akāl Chāṇā / Merging of Bhai Mardana Ji
summary: The life of Bhai Mardana Ji, the Muslim minstrel who played the rabab for Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji on every udasi, and how Sikhs remember his passing.
body:
This day remembers the passing of Bhai Mardana Ji, the companion of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji for most of his life and the first musician of the Sikh tradition. Sikhs speak of his akal chalana, his departure into the timeless, and of his merging with the Divine.

## The minstrel of Talwandi

Bhai Mardana Ji was born in 1459 at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib, into a family of Muslim mirasis, hereditary musicians. He was about ten years older than Guru Nanak Dev Ji and knew him from childhood. When the Guru set out on his long journeys, the udasis, Bhai Mardana Ji went with him, carrying the rabab, a stringed instrument. The Guru sang the bani as it came to him, and Bhai Mardana Ji set it to music; the Janamsakhis tell that the Guru would say, Mardana, play the rabab, the bani is coming.

## Companion on every road

For more than two decades the two travelled together, east to Assam, south to Sri Lanka, north into the mountains and west to Mecca and Baghdad. The Janamsakhis tell many stories of their journeys, of hunger and danger shared, and of the Guru's affection for his friend. In the Vaar in Raag Bihagara of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, three shaloks of Guru Nanak Dev Ji are headed with his companion's name, Mardana. Accounts differ on where he died: some name Kartarpur, others the banks of the Kurram in Afghanistan during the journeys. Tradition holds that the Guru performed his last rites himself.

## How he is remembered

His descendants, the rababis, kept singing kirtan at Sikh shrines for centuries. Sikhs remember his devotion with kirtan, often with the rabab and other string instruments in the old style, and with Ardas in gurdwaras.
label: Joti Jot

title: Shaheedi Purab – Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
summary: In 1606 Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji was tortured to death in Lahore on Jahangir's orders. Why it happened, Gurdwara Dera Sahib, and why Sikhs serve cold water on the day.
body:
The Shaheedi Purab of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji remembers the martyrdom of the fifth Sikh Guru in Lahore in 1606. He was the first of the Gurus to give his life, and his shaheedi shaped everything that followed in Sikh history.

## Why the Guru was arrested

By 1606 the Sikh community had grown into a strong and organised body around Sri Harmandir Sahib and the Adi Granth, and the Guru's teaching drew people of every faith. The emperor Jahangir, newly on the throne, wrote in his own memoirs that he had long wished to put an end to the Guru's influence. When his rebel son Khusrau passed through Punjab and was received at the Guru's court, Jahangir had the pretext he needed. The Guru was summoned to Lahore, fined heavily and asked to remove passages from the Granth; he refused both.

## The torture in Lahore

Over several days in the summer heat, the Guru was made to sit on a red-hot iron plate while burning sand was poured over him, and was boiled in a cauldron. Tradition remembers that the Muslim saint Mian Mir, who had laid the foundation stone of Sri Harmandir Sahib, offered to intervene, and the Guru asked him not to, accepting the Divine Will as sweet. He was then taken to the river Ravi, where his body disappeared into the water. Gurdwara Dera Sahib now stands at the place, beside the Lahore Fort.

## The chhabeel

Because the Guru was tortured in the burning heat of summer, Sikhs mark the day by setting up chhabeels along roads and outside gurdwaras, serving cold sweetened water and milk to every passer-by, whatever their faith. Gurdwaras hold Akhand Paath and kirtan, and many sangats recite Sukhmani Sahib, the Guru's own bani of peace.

title: Shaheedi Purab – Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji
summary: In 1675 Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji gave his life at Chandni Chowk, Delhi, for the freedom of others to follow their faith. The story of Hind di Chadar and the day.
body:
The Shaheedi Purab of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji remembers the martyrdom of the ninth Sikh Guru at Chandni Chowk in Delhi in November 1675. He gave his life not for his own faith but for the right of others to practise theirs, and Sikhs remember him as Hind di Chadar, the shield of India.

## The plea of the Kashmiri Pandits

Under the emperor Aurangzeb, the Pandits of Kashmir were being pressed to convert to Islam. A group led by Pandit Kirpa Ram came to the Guru at Anandpur Sahib and asked for his help. The Guru told them to tell the authorities that if Guru Tegh Bahadur could be made to convert, they would all follow. He then set out for Delhi with a few companions and was arrested on the way.

## Chandni Chowk

Held in Delhi, the Guru was given three choices: accept Islam, perform a miracle to prove his holiness, or die. He refused the first two. To break his resolve, his companions Bhai Mati Das Ji, Bhai Sati Das Ji and Bhai Dyala Ji were put to death before his eyes. On the day, the Guru was beheaded in the open at Chandni Chowk. In the confusion of a storm, Bhai Jaita Ji carried the Guru's head to Anandpur Sahib, and Bhai Lakhi Shah Vanjara took his body to his house and set the house alight to cremate it.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib marks the place of the martyrdom, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib the place of the cremation. Sangats hold Akhand Paath, kirtan, katha and Nagar Kirtan, and many recite his saloks, which close the reading of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

title: Shaheedi – Bhai Dyala Ji, Bhai Mati Das Ji & Bhai Sati Das Ji
summary: Three Sikhs arrested with Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji were put to death before him in Delhi in 1675: sawn, burnt and boiled. Who they were and how they are remembered.
body:
This day remembers three Sikhs who were put to death in Delhi in November 1675, in front of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, so that the sight of their suffering might break the Guru's resolve. It did not, and neither did theirs.

## Who they were

Bhai Mati Das Ji and Bhai Sati Das Ji were brothers from the village of Kariala, near Jhelum, from a family that had served the Gurus for generations. Bhai Mati Das Ji was the Guru's diwan, his steward, and Bhai Sati Das Ji wrote Persian for the Guru. Bhai Dyala Ji, from Alipur near Multan, was a close companion of the Guru and of his family. All three travelled with the Guru from Anandpur Sahib and were arrested with him.

## The martyrdoms

Bhai Mati Das Ji was asked to give up his faith and refused. He was tied between two posts and sawn in two from the head down, reciting Japji Sahib as long as he could. Bhai Dyala Ji was boiled alive in a cauldron, and Bhai Sati Das Ji was wrapped in cotton soaked in oil and set alight. Each remained calm, in remembrance of the Divine, to the end. The Guru's own shaheedi followed shortly after at Chandni Chowk.

## How they are remembered

Their names are spoken in every Ardas, among those who were sawn apart and boiled alive and did not waver. The Bhai Mati Das Museum stands opposite Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Delhi, and a chowk there is named after the three. Sangats remember them with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib, in the days before the Guru's Shaheedi Purab.

title: Shaheedi – Bhai Jivan Singh (Bhai Jaita Ji)
summary: Bhai Jaita Ji carried the head of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji from Delhi to Anandpur Sahib in 1675, later became Bhai Jivan Singh, and fell at Chamkaur in 1704.
body:
This day remembers Bhai Jaita Ji, later Bhai Jivan Singh Ji, whose courage in 1675 gave the Sikhs one of the most moving moments in their history, and who gave his own life in the battles of December 1704.

## The head of the Guru

Bhai Jaita Ji belonged to a family of sweepers, the community the caste order held lowest, who had long served the Gurus. He was in Delhi when Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji was beheaded at Chandni Chowk in November 1675. No one dared claim the body. In the confusion of a sudden storm, Bhai Jaita Ji took up the Guru's head, wrapped it, and carried it in secret, travelling by night, all the way to Kiratpur and Anandpur Sahib. The young Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji received it, embraced him, and blessed him with the words Rangrete Guru ke bete, the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons. The head was cremated where Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib, Anandpur Sahib, now stands.

## Bhai Jivan Singh

Bhai Jaita Ji took Amrit at the creation of the Khalsa in 1699 and became Bhai Jivan Singh Ji. He was a skilled warrior and a poet, and served close to the Guru at Anandpur Sahib, where he is remembered as commanding Sikhs in its defence. When the Guru left Anandpur Sahib in December 1704, Bhai Jivan Singh Ji rode with him, and he fell fighting at Chamkaur Sahib, among the Singhs who held back the Mughal army.

## How he is remembered

Sikhs remember him with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Anandpur Sahib and Chamkaur Sahib, and as a reminder that the Guru's house knows no caste.

title: Saka Chamkaur Sahib
summary: In December 1704, at the garhi of Chamkaur, the elder sons of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, Baba Ajit Singh Ji and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, gave their lives. The story of the saka.
body:
Saka Chamkaur Sahib remembers the battle at Chamkaur in December 1704, in which the two elder sons of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, Baba Ajit Singh Ji, aged about eighteen, and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, aged about fourteen, gave their lives with a small band of Singhs against a vast Mughal army.

## The flight from Anandpur

After a long siege, the Guru left Anandpur Sahib on promises of safe passage sworn on the Quran and on a cow. The promises were broken and the Sikhs were attacked as they crossed the flooded Sirsa river, where the Guru's family was scattered. The Guru, his two elder sons and about forty Singhs reached Chamkaur and took shelter in a mud fortress, a garhi, belonging to a local landowner. By morning they were surrounded.

## Five at a time

With only a few arrows and swords left, the Singhs went out of the garhi in groups of five to meet the besiegers. Baba Ajit Singh Ji asked his father's permission to go, and the Guru armed him himself. He fought until he fell. Seeing this, Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, still a boy, asked to follow his brother; tradition remembers the Guru embracing him and sending him out, and watching from the garhi as he too fell. Through the day the Singhs held the army back, among them three of the Panj Pyare, Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji, Bhai Himmat Singh Ji and Bhai Sahib Singh Ji.

## How the saka is remembered

Gurdwara Qatalgarh Sahib marks the place where the Sahibzade and the Singhs fell, and Gurdwara Garhi Sahib the fortress. The Shaheedi Jorh Mela at Chamkaur Sahib draws great sangats for kirtan, katha and Ardas, and many Sikh families spend these December days in simple living, sleeping on the floor and keeping from celebrations.

title: Shaheedi – Bhai Sangat Singh Ji
summary: When the Guru Khalsa asked Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji to leave the garhi of Chamkaur, Bhai Sangat Singh Ji stayed behind wearing the Guru's kalgi, and fell the next day.
body:
This day remembers Bhai Sangat Singh Ji, one of the last Singhs left in the garhi of Chamkaur Sahib in December 1704. When the Guru left the besieged fortress at night, he stayed behind in the Guru's place, so that the army outside would believe the Guru was still within.

## The night at Chamkaur

By the end of the first day at Chamkaur, both elder Sahibzade and most of the Singhs had fallen, and only a handful remained in the mud fortress. Acting as the Panj Pyare, five of them asked Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji to escape so that he could continue to lead the Panth, and the Guru obeyed the Khalsa. Before he went, tradition remembers that he placed his kalgi, the plume he wore in his turban, and his dress on Bhai Sangat Singh Ji, who resembled him in height and features, and seated him in his place.

## Holding the garhi

The Guru slipped out in the darkness with three Singhs. In the morning the besiegers attacked the garhi expecting to take the Guru, and met Bhai Sangat Singh Ji and the few remaining Singhs, who fought until every one of them fell. Some accounts hold that the commanders, finding the body in the Guru's dress, believed for a time that the Guru had been killed, which gave him precious hours to get away towards the Machhiwara forest.

## How he is remembered

Many accounts give Bhai Sangat Singh Ji's earlier name as Bhai Sangtia Ji, and some link him to the family of Bhai Jaita Ji. He is remembered at Chamkaur Sahib with kirtan and Ardas during the Shaheedi Jorh Mela, and as an example of selfless sacrifice for the Guru and the Panth.

title: Shaheedi – Chhote Sahibzade and Mata Gujri Ji
summary: In December 1704 Baba Zorawar Singh Ji, 9, and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, 6, were bricked into a wall at Sirhind, and Mata Gujri Ji passed away in the Thanda Burj. The story.
body:
Saka Sirhind remembers the martyrdom in December 1704 of the two youngest sons of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, Baba Zorawar Singh Ji, aged nine, and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, aged six, and of their grandmother, Mata Gujri Ji. It is among the most sorrowful days in the Sikh year.

## Betrayed

When the Guru's family was scattered at the flooded Sirsa river, Mata Gujri Ji and the two youngest Sahibzade were separated from the rest. Their former cook, Gangu, offered them shelter in his village, Saheri, and then betrayed them to the authorities for a reward. They were taken to Sirhind and held in the Thanda Burj, an open tower, through bitter winter nights. Tradition remembers that Bhai Moti Ram Mehra, a servant in the governor's kitchens, risked his life to bring them milk.

## The court of Wazir Khan

The Sahibzade were brought before Wazir Khan, the governor of Sirhind, and offered wealth and safety if they would give up their faith. They refused, entering the court with a loud Fateh. Sher Mohammad Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla, protested that children should not be punished for their father, a protest Sikhs still honour as the haa da naara. The governor ordered them to be bricked alive into a wall; when the wall collapsed, they were put to death. On hearing the news, Mata Gujri Ji passed away in the tower.

## How the day is remembered

Diwan Todar Mal, a wealthy merchant, bought the land for their cremation by covering it with gold coins. Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib marks the place, and Gurdwara Jyoti Sarup the cremation. The Shaheedi Jorh Mela at Fatehgarh Sahib draws vast sangats, and many families keep the week simply, in remembrance.

title: Shaheedi – Baba Banda Singh Bahadur Ji
summary: Baba Banda Singh Bahadur took Sirhind in 1710, set up Sikh rule from Lohgarh and gave land to those who tilled it. His capture and his martyrdom in Delhi in June 1716.
body:
This day remembers the martyrdom of Baba Banda Singh Bahadur in Delhi in June 1716. In the eight years after he met Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, he led the Khalsa to its first great victories and set up the first Sikh rule in Punjab.

## From Madho Das to Banda Singh

Born Lachhman Dev in 1670 in Rajouri, he became an ascetic called Madho Das and kept a hermitage at Nanded on the Godavari. In 1708 Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji came to Nanded; tradition remembers that Madho Das tried to overawe the Guru with his powers and failed, and fell at his feet saying he was the Guru's banda, his servant. He took Amrit as Banda Singh, and the Guru sent him to Punjab with five arrows, a nishan sahib, a drum and a council of five Singhs.

## The victories

Sikhs rallied to him across Punjab. In 1709 he took Samana, and in May 1710 he defeated Wazir Khan, the governor responsible for the death of the younger Sahibzade, at Chappar Chiri, and took Sirhind. He made Lohgarh, near Sadhaura, his capital, struck coins in the name of Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Guru Gobind Singh Ji, and abolished the zamindari system, giving land to those who tilled it.

## Capture and martyrdom

In 1715 a huge Mughal army besieged him at Gurdas Nangal for eight months until the starving garrison was overrun. He was taken to Delhi in an iron cage with hundreds of Sikhs, who were executed day after day, not one accepting the offer of life for conversion. On the day, his young son Ajai Singh was killed before his eyes, and Banda Singh was tortured and put to death. Gurdwaras hold kirtan and Ardas in his memory.
label: Shaheedi

title: Shaheedi Purab – Bhai Mani Singh Ji
summary: Bhai Mani Singh Ji wrote out Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Damdama Sahib and served as granthi at Amritsar. In 1738 he was cut apart joint by joint in Lahore. His story.
body:
The Shaheedi Purab of Bhai Mani Singh Ji remembers the martyrdom in Lahore in 1738 of one of the most learned and devoted Sikhs of his age, who served the Gurus for most of his life and is named in every Ardas among those who were cut apart, joint by joint.

## A lifetime of service

Bhai Mani Singh Ji came to the court of Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji as a child and grew up beside the young Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, becoming his close companion. He took Amrit in 1699, and many of his brothers and sons gave their lives in the battles of the Guru's time. At Damdama Sahib in 1706 he was the scribe who wrote out Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the Guru dictated, adding the bani of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji. After the Guru, Mata Sundari Ji sent him to Amritsar as granthi of Sri Harmandir Sahib, where he settled disputes in the Panth and preached for many years. Tradition also credits him with gathering the bani of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji.

## The Diwali tax

In 1738 he sought permission from Zakariya Khan, the governor of Lahore, for Sikhs to gather at Amritsar for Diwali, and agreed to pay a heavy tax from the offerings. Fearing an attack, the governor sent troops, the sangat scattered, and the tax could not be raised. Bhai Mani Singh Ji was arrested and taken to Lahore.

## The shaheedi

Offered his life if he accepted Islam, he refused. He was sentenced to be cut apart joint by joint, and when the executioner began with his wrist, tradition remembers he held out his hand at the fingers, reminding him of his orders. He bore it in calm remembrance of the Divine. Gurdwaras hold kirtan, katha and Ardas in his memory.
label: Shaheedi

title: Bhai Taru Singh Ji
summary: Bhai Taru Singh Ji of Poohla fed Sikhs hiding in the forests and, in 1745, chose to have his scalp removed rather than cut his kes. His life, his shaheedi, and both his days.
body:
Bhai Taru Singh Ji is remembered twice in the Nanakshahi calendar, at his birth anniversary and at his Shaheedi Purab. His story, from the dark years of the eighteenth century, is the clearest example in Sikh history of devotion to the kes, the uncut hair that is part of the Sikh form.

## The farmer of Poohla

Bhai Taru Singh Ji was born in 1720 at Poohla, a village near Amritsar, and lived with his widowed mother and his sister. In those years the governors of Lahore had put a price on the head of every Sikh, and many Singhs lived in the forests and deserts. Bhai Taru Singh Ji farmed his land and quietly shared what he grew with them, giving them food and shelter.

## Arrest

In 1745 an informer, Harbhagat Niranjania, reported him to Zakariya Khan, the governor of Lahore, for helping the rebels. He was arrested and brought to Lahore. The governor offered him his life if he would accept Islam and cut his hair. He refused. Tradition remembers that when told his kes would be cut, he answered that his hair would go with his scalp, and asked for no other mercy.

## The shaheedi

On the governor's orders his scalp was removed with a sharp blade. He bore it calmly, reciting the bani. He lived on for some days, and tradition holds that Zakariya Khan fell ill and died before him. Gurdwara Shaheed Bhai Taru Singh Ji in Lahore marks the place.

## How he is remembered

Sikhs remember him with kirtan, katha and Ardas on both days. Many gurdwaras use the occasion to speak about the kes and the dastar, and young Sikhs often hold turban-tying camps in his memory.

title: Baba Deep Singh Ji
summary: Baba Deep Singh Ji copied Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Damdama Sahib, led the Shaheedan Misl, and in 1757, aged 75, fell fighting to free Sri Harmandir Sahib. His two days.
body:
Baba Deep Singh Ji is remembered twice in the Nanakshahi calendar, at his birth anniversary in winter and at his Shaheedi Purab in autumn. He was both a scholar of the Guru's bani and one of the bravest warriors of the eighteenth century.

## Scholar of Damdama Sahib

Born in 1682 at Pahuwind, near Amritsar, Deep Singh Ji came to Anandpur Sahib as a young man and took Amrit from Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji. He learned Gurmukhi and the bani there, and stayed at Damdama Sahib with Bhai Mani Singh Ji while Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji was written out. He later made several handwritten copies of the scripture, sent to the Takhts, and taught at the centre of learning that grew at Damdama Sahib, remembered as the Guru Ki Kashi.

## The Shaheedan Misl

In the 1730s, when the Khalsa was organised into misls, Baba Deep Singh Ji led the Shaheedan Misl, its members sworn to give their lives for the Panth. He fought alongside Banda Singh Bahadur and in many later battles.

## The last battle

In 1757 Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces, under Jahan Khan, desecrated Sri Harmandir Sahib and filled its sarovar with debris. Baba Deep Singh Ji, then seventy-five, vowed to celebrate Diwali at Amritsar. He drew a line in the earth, asked those ready to die to cross it, and set out, thousands joining him on the way. Near Amritsar, at Gohalwar, he was gravely wounded. Sikh tradition remembers that, holding his head on his palm, he fought on to reach the sacred precincts. Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Baba Deep Singh Ji marks the place, and sangats gather there for kirtan and Ardas on both days.

title: Shaheedi – Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji
summary: In December 1764 Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji and about thirty Singhs stayed at Amritsar to defend Sri Harmandir Sahib against Ahmad Shah Abdali's army and fell to the last man.
body:
This day remembers Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji and about thirty Singhs who stayed at Amritsar in December 1764 to defend Sri Harmandir Sahib against the army of Ahmad Shah Abdali, knowing they could not win, and fell to the last man.

## A Nihang of the Shaheedan Misl

Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji was born in 1688 at Lil, near Khem Karan, and is remembered as having taken Amrit as a young man, by many accounts from Bhai Mani Singh Ji. He spent his life in the service of the Panth and of Sri Harmandir Sahib, and was a Nihang of the Shaheedan Misl, the band once led by Baba Deep Singh Ji.

## The seventh invasion

In the winter of 1764 Ahmad Shah Abdali crossed into Punjab on his seventh invasion and marched on Amritsar. Most of the Khalsa forces were away, and the Sikhs in the city were few. Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji, then in his seventies, chose to stay and defend the Guru's house. He and about thirty companions prepared themselves, did Ardas, and waited at the complex as the invading army approached.

## The last stand

When the army of thousands reached the precincts, the Singhs came out to meet it at the gates and fought until every one of them fell. The Persian chronicler Qazi Nur Muhammad, who travelled with Abdali's army, wrote of the few Sikhs who came out to face it, with no fear of death. Abdali's forces then demolished Sri Harmandir Sahib, which the Khalsa rebuilt soon after.

## How the day is remembered

Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji, behind Sri Akal Takht Sahib, marks the place where they were cremated, and sangats remember them there with kirtan and Ardas.
