title: Wadda Ghallughara – Kup Rohira
summary: In February 1762 Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces caught a Sikh caravan near Kup Rohira, and tens of thousands were killed in a day. The story, and the Jorh Melas that remember it.
body:
The Wadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust, took place on 5 February 1762 near the villages of Kup and Rohira, in today's Malerkotla district. In a single day the forces of Ahmad Shah Abdali killed a very large number of Sikhs, many of them women, children and the elderly. Sikh sources speak of tens of thousands; historians usually give figures between ten and thirty thousand. It is remembered as one of the darkest days in Sikh history.

## The caravan

Early in 1762 the Sikhs were moving their families south from the Majha to the safety of the Malwa desert, near Barnala. Abdali, on his sixth invasion, made a forced march from Lahore with his army and joined the forces of the governor of Sirhind and the Nawab of Malerkotla, surprising the camp at Kup before dawn.

## A moving wall

The Khalsa, led by Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Charat Singh Sukerchakia, formed a ring around the caravan of non-combatants and fought as they marched, mile after mile, through the whole day. Jassa Singh Ahluwalia was wounded many times. By evening, near Gahil and Kutba-Bahmania, the survivors reached water and the attackers fell back. Abdali went on to blow up Sri Harmandir Sahib. Yet within months the Khalsa had regrouped and defeated his forces, and within two years they ruled Sirhind.

## How it is remembered

The day is observed with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas. Sangats gather at the memorial at Kup Rohira, built at the site of the massacre, and at Gahil in Barnala district, where an annual Jorh Mela remembers the end of that day's march.

title: Shaheedi – Bhai Subeg Singh & Bhai Shahbaz Singh
summary: In 1745 Bhai Subeg Singh, once an official of Lahore, and his teenage son Bhai Shahbaz Singh were broken on the wheel for refusing to give up their faith. Their story.
body:
This day remembers Bhai Subeg Singh and his son, Bhai Shahbaz Singh, who were put to death in Lahore in 1745 on the charkhri, a wheel set with blades, for refusing to give up the Sikh faith. Every Ardas recalls those who were broken on the wheel and did not waver. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps the day on a fixed solar date.

## A Sikh at the governor's court

Bhai Subeg Singh, from Jambar near Lahore, was a learned man who knew Persian and served the Mughal administration of Lahore as an official and, at times, as its go-between with the Khalsa. In 1733, when the governor Zakariya Khan offered the Sikhs a jagir and the title of Nawab in an attempt to make peace, it was Bhai Subeg Singh who carried the offer to the Khalsa, which conferred the title on Kapur Singh, remembered ever after as Nawab Kapur Singh.

## The son's refusal

His son, Shahbaz Singh, was a bright boy of about eighteen studying with a Muslim teacher, a qazi, who wanted him to convert and, when he would not, accused him of insulting the Prophet. The boy was arrested. When his father went to plead for him, he too was seized. Both were offered their lives if they accepted Islam; both refused.

## The wheel

Father and son were tied to the charkhri and turned on it until their bodies were broken. Tradition remembers that each encouraged the other to remain steadfast to the end, and that the governor, Zakariya Khan, died in the same year. Gurdwaras remember them with kirtan, katha and Ardas, and their story is often told to young Sikhs as an example of faith that does not bend.

title: Saka Nankana Sahib
summary: On 20 February 1921 a jatha led by Bhai Lachhman Singh Dharowali was massacred by the mahant's men at Nankana Sahib. What happened, and how it changed the gurdwaras.
body:
Saka Nankana Sahib remembers the massacre of 20 February 1921 at Gurdwara Janam Asthan, the birthplace of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, where a peaceful jatha of Sikhs was killed by armed men hired by the mahant who controlled the shrine. It is one of the defining events of the Gurdwara Reform Movement.

## The mahants

In the nineteenth century many historic gurdwaras had come under hereditary mahants, custodians who treated them as private property, often with the backing of the British authorities. Some brought in practices against Sikh teaching and kept the offerings for themselves. At Nankana Sahib, Mahant Narain Das was notorious for the misconduct allowed at the shrine. In 1920 the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee was formed to bring the gurdwaras under the Panth's own care.

## The morning of 20 February

A jatha led by Bhai Lachhman Singh Dharowali entered Gurdwara Janam Asthan early in the morning and sat before Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji in kirtan. The mahant had prepared for them with armed men. They opened fire, attacked the Sikhs with swords and axes, and burned many of the bodies, some still alive. Bhai Lachhman Singh Ji was tied to a tree and burnt. Bhai Dalip Singh Ji, who came to plead for peace, was shot. Official figures counted well over a hundred dead; Sikh accounts give more.

## What followed

The saka shook the whole Panth and turned opinion in India against the mahants. Within days the shrine was handed to the Sikhs, and the reform movement gathered force, leading to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. Sangats remember the shaheeds with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, at Nankana Sahib and everywhere.

imageCaption: Gurdwara Janam Asthan, Nankana Sahib, the site of the saka

title: Shaheedi – Sardar Kartar Singh Sarabha Ji
summary: Kartar Singh Sarabha joined the Ghadar Party in America, returned to Punjab to raise a revolt, and was hanged in Lahore in November 1915 at nineteen. His life.
body:
This day remembers Kartar Singh Sarabha, a young Sikh of the Ghadar movement who was hanged by the British in Lahore on 16 November 1915, aged nineteen. Bhagat Singh later kept his photograph with him and spoke of him as his guide.

## From Sarabha to San Francisco

Kartar Singh was born in 1896 in the village of Sarabha, near Ludhiana, and lost his father as a child. After school he went to the United States in 1912 to study at the University of California at Berkeley. Among the Punjabi labourers on the Pacific coast, many of them Sikhs, he met the racism and humiliation they faced as subjects of a colonised country, and joined the Ghadar Party when it was founded in 1913. He helped print and send out its newspaper, Ghadar, in Punjabi and Urdu.

## The planned uprising

When the First World War began in 1914, the Ghadar leaders called on Indians abroad to return and raise a revolt while Britain was at war. Kartar Singh came back to Punjab and travelled tirelessly, meeting soldiers in cantonments, gathering arms and preparing for an uprising set for February 1915. The plan was betrayed by an informer, and arrests followed across Punjab.

## Trial and execution

He was arrested and tried in the first Lahore Conspiracy Case. In court he spoke openly of his aims, and was sentenced to death with six companions. He was hanged in Lahore Central Jail. Tradition remembers his calm and his good spirits in his last days.

## How he is remembered

He is remembered with tributes, Ardas and gatherings, above all in his village, where a memorial and his ancestral home stand, and in gurdwaras that keep the SGPC's calendar.
label: Shaheedi

title: Shaheedi – Sardar Udham Singh Ji
summary: Udham Singh never forgot the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919. In 1940 he shot Michael O'Dwyer in London and was hanged at Pentonville on 31 July. His life and his day.
body:
This day remembers Sardar Udham Singh, who was hanged at Pentonville Prison in London on 31 July 1940 for the killing of Sir Michael O'Dwyer, the man who had governed Punjab at the time of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

## An orphan of Sunam

Udham Singh was born in 1899 at Sunam, in today's Sangrur district, and lost both parents young. He and his brother were raised at the Central Khalsa Orphanage in Amritsar, where he grew up close to Sri Harmandir Sahib.

## Jallianwala Bagh

On Vaisakhi, 13 April 1919, thousands gathered at Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden near Sri Harmandir Sahib, many of them pilgrims for the festival. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer marched in troops, blocked the exit and ordered them to fire into the crowd without warning. Hundreds were killed and many more wounded. The Lieutenant Governor of Punjab, Sir Michael O'Dwyer, endorsed the firing. Udham Singh, then a young man, is remembered as having vowed to answer it.

## Caxton Hall

For years he moved between India, Africa, America and England, joined the Ghadar movement, and served time in prison. On 13 March 1940, at a meeting at Caxton Hall in London, he shot O'Dwyer dead. At his trial he gave his name as Ram Mohammad Singh Azad, joining the names of India's faiths, and spoke against British rule. He was hanged at Pentonville.

## How he is remembered

In 1974 his remains were brought back to India and cremated at Sunam. He is remembered as a shaheed of the freedom struggle with tributes, Ardas and gatherings across Punjab, above all at Sunam and at Jallianwala Bagh.

imageCaption: The Jallianwala Bagh memorial, Amritsar

title: Shaheedi – Bhagat Singh
summary: Bhagat Singh was hanged in Lahore on 23 March 1931 with Rajguru and Sukhdev, aged twenty-three. His Sikh family, his revolutionary life and how Shaheedi Divas is kept.
body:
This day remembers Bhagat Singh, the young revolutionary who was hanged by the British in Lahore Central Jail on 23 March 1931, together with Sukhdev Thapar and Shivaram Rajguru. He was twenty-three. The day is kept across India as Shaheedi Divas, and the SGPC's calendar keeps it on a fixed solar date.

## A family of the freedom struggle

Bhagat Singh was born in 1907 at Banga, in Lyallpur district, now in Pakistan, into a Sikh family whose ancestral home was Khatkar Kalan in Punjab. His father and his uncles were involved in the movements against British rule, and the family's stories of the Ghadar martyrs, above all Kartar Singh Sarabha, shaped him. As a boy of twelve he visited Jallianwala Bagh after the massacre of 1919.

## The revolutionary

In Lahore he read widely, wrote for Punjabi and Urdu papers and helped found the Naujawan Bharat Sabha and the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. After the death of Lala Lajpat Rai following a police baton charge in 1928, he and his companions killed a British police officer, John Saunders. In 1929 he and Batukeshwar Dutt threw harmless smoke bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi and courted arrest, using their trial to put their ideas before the country. In jail he led a long hunger strike for the rights of political prisoners and kept writing.

## The execution

He, Sukhdev and Rajguru were sentenced to death and hanged a day earlier than announced. Their bodies were secretly cremated on the bank of the Sutlej near Hussainiwala, where the National Martyrs Memorial now stands.

## How he is remembered

He is remembered with tributes and gatherings, above all at Hussainiwala and at Khatkar Kalan.
label: Shaheedi

title: Shaheedi Saka Paonta Sahib
summary: Paonta Sahib, where Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji lived and wrote by the Yamuna, and the Saka of 1964, when Sikhs were killed in police firing at the gurdwara. The history.
body:
The Shaheedi Saka Paonta Sahib remembers the Sikhs who were killed in police firing at Gurdwara Sri Paonta Sahib in 1964, during a dispute over the management and maryada of the gurdwara. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps the day so that their sacrifice is not forgotten.

## The Guru's city by the Yamuna

Paonta Sahib stands on the banks of the Yamuna in the Sirmaur district of Himachal Pradesh. Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji came here in 1685 at the invitation of the Raja of Sirmaur and lived here for about four years. The name is often explained as the place where the Guru set his foot. These were years of learning and writing: the Guru composed bani here, and gathered fifty-two poets at his court, where the Kavi Darbar Asthan still stands and a poetry gathering is held each year. In 1688 the hill rajas attacked him at Bhangani, nearby, and the Sikhs, with Pir Budhu Shah and his sons and disciples fighting beside them, won the battle.

## The saka of 1964

In the decades after Independence, control of the gurdwara and the way its services were conducted became the subject of a long dispute. In 1964 the dispute ended in police firing at the gurdwara, and a number of Sikhs lost their lives. The Panth remembers them as shaheeds who gave their lives for the sanctity of the Guru's place.

## How the day is observed

It is observed with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas for those who gave their lives, at Paonta Sahib and in gurdwaras elsewhere. It is also a day to remember the sangat's care for the Guru's historic places, and the long struggle to keep them in the Panth's own hands.
label: Shaheedi
imageCaption: Gurdwara Sri Paonta Sahib, Sirmaur, Himachal Pradesh

title: Akal Takht Sahib Ghallughara / martyrdoms of 1984
summary: In June 1984 the Indian Army entered the Sri Harmandir Sahib complex during a Gurpurab. Sri Akal Takht Sahib was destroyed and many died. How Sikhs remember the Third Ghallughara.
body:
In the first week of June 1984 the Indian Army entered the complex of Sri Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar in a military operation, codenamed Blue Star, that also struck dozens of other gurdwaras across Punjab. Sikhs remember it as the Teeja Ghallughara, the Third Great Massacre, after the two of the eighteenth century.

## The days of the operation

The operation began during the Shaheedi Gurpurab of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, when the complex was full of pilgrims, many of them families who had come for the day. Punjab was placed under curfew and cut off from the outside world. Armed militants, led by Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale and the former general Shabeg Singh, had fortified Sri Akal Takht Sahib, and the fighting lasted several days, with the army bringing in tanks. Sri Akal Takht Sahib was heavily damaged, the Sikh Reference Library, with its handwritten manuscripts and historical records, was burned, and Sri Harmandir Sahib itself was struck by gunfire.

## The cost

The government's figures counted several hundred civilians and militants killed and many soldiers; other estimates are far higher. Among the dead were pilgrims, women and children, and sevadars. Many Sikhs who had no part in the fighting were held for long afterwards. The operation, and the killing of Sikhs in Delhi and other cities that November, left a lasting wound.

## How the day is observed

Sri Akal Takht Sahib was later rebuilt by kar seva of the Panth. The anniversary is observed with Akhand Paath and Ardas at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, and with remembrance in gurdwaras around the world. Views of the political events differ widely; the day itself is kept as one of mourning and remembrance.
label: Shaheedi
imageCaption: Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, rebuilt after 1984

title: Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale
summary: The head of the Damdami Taksal from 1977, killed at Sri Akal Takht Sahib in June 1984 with Bhai Amrik Singh Ji. His life, the views of it, and the two days the SGPC keeps.
body:
The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps two days for Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale: his birth anniversary in June, and the anniversary of his death at Sri Akal Takht Sahib in June 1984, which it marks as a shaheedi together with that of Bhai Amrik Singh Ji. His life remains one of the most debated in modern Sikh history.

## The preacher

Jarnail Singh was born in 1947 at Rode, in Faridkot district, into a farming family, and was sent as a boy to study at the Damdami Taksal, a seminary of Sikh learning that traces its origins to Damdama Sahib. In 1977 he became its head. Travelling from village to village, he became widely known as a preacher who urged young Sikhs to take Amrit, keep their kes and give up alcohol and drugs, and many responded.

## The political struggle

In the early 1980s he became a leading figure in the agitation over Punjab's demands, at a time of rising violence in the state, and from 1982 he lived in the Sri Harmandir Sahib complex, later at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. He was killed there during the army operation of June 1984, together with Bhai Amrik Singh Ji, president of the All India Sikh Students Federation and son of the earlier head of the Taksal, and with many others.

## Differing views

Many Sikhs regard him as a shaheed who stood for the dignity of the Panth; others, in India and beyond, hold him responsible for the violence of those years. Hazri follows the SGPC's calendar in listing both days. They are observed with Akhand Paath and Ardas, especially at Sri Akal Takht Sahib and at the Damdami Taksal headquarters at Mehta Chowk.

title: Shaheedi – Sant Harchand Singh Ji Longowal
summary: Sant Harchand Singh Ji Longowal led the Akali Dal and the Dharam Yudh Morcha, signed the Punjab Accord in July 1985, and was shot dead at Sherpur weeks later. His life.
body:
This day remembers Sant Harchand Singh Ji Longowal, president of the Shiromani Akali Dal, who was shot dead on 20 August 1985 while addressing a gathering at a gurdwara in Sherpur, near Sangrur, less than a month after signing an accord meant to bring peace to Punjab.

## A preacher from Longowal

Harchand Singh was born in 1932 in the Sangrur district and grew up in the village of Longowal. He studied the Guru's bani from a young age, became a kirtani and preacher, and was respected for his simple way of life. He was drawn into the Akali movement, took part in the morchas of the 1970s against the Emergency, and rose to lead the Shiromani Akali Dal.

## The Dharam Yudh Morcha

From 1982 he led the Dharam Yudh Morcha, a mass campaign for the demands set out in the Anandpur Sahib Resolution, among them the transfer of Chandigarh to Punjab, a fair share of river waters and greater autonomy for the states. Tens of thousands of volunteers courted arrest. After the army operation of June 1984 he was among the Akali leaders detained.

## The Punjab Accord

Released in 1985, he chose the path of negotiation. On 24 July 1985 he and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi signed the Punjab Accord, which promised to settle many of the state's long-standing demands. Many welcomed it as a hope of peace after years of bloodshed; others opposed it. On 20 August he was killed by gunmen at Sherpur.

## How the day is observed

The SGPC's calendar keeps his shaheedi, and it is observed with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, especially at Longowal, where a memorial stands.
label: Shaheedi

title: Shaheedi – Bhai Beant Singh Ji
summary: Bhai Beant Singh, a guard of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, shot her on 31 October 1984 and was killed in custody. The events, the killings that followed, and the day.
body:
The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps 31 October as the shaheedi of Bhai Beant Singh. It is one of the most contested days in the calendar, and for many Sikhs it is above all the beginning of the November 1984 killings.

## The events of 31 October 1984

Beant Singh was a sub-inspector of the Delhi Police posted to the security staff of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Like many Sikhs, he was deeply affected by the army operation at Sri Harmandir Sahib in June that year. On the morning of 31 October 1984, at the Prime Minister's residence in New Delhi, he and another guard, Satwant Singh, shot her as she walked to an interview. Beant Singh was shot dead by other security personnel in custody the same morning. Satwant Singh was wounded, tried and later hanged, along with Kehar Singh.

## The killings that followed

Over the next days, mobs in Delhi and other cities hunted down Sikhs, killing thousands, burning homes and gurdwaras, while the authorities were slow to act. Official enquiries later found that political figures had helped organise some of the violence. Families in Delhi's resettlement colonies bore the worst of it, and justice for the victims took decades, where it came at all.

## How the day is observed

Views of the assassination differ sharply. The SGPC marks Beant Singh's death as a shaheedi, and the day is observed with Ardas at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. Many Sikhs also use these days to remember the innocent people killed in November 1984, at memorials such as the Wall of Truth at Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib in Delhi, and with Akhand Paath and Ardas in gurdwaras around the world.
label: Shaheedi

title: Birth anniversary – Sahibzada Baba Ajit Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sahibzada Baba Ajit Singh Ji, born at Paonta Sahib in 1687: his youth at Anandpur Sahib, the battle of Nuh, and his shaheedi at Chamkaur.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Sahibzada Baba Ajit Singh Ji, the eldest son of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, born at Paonta Sahib in 1687 to Mata Sundari Ji. He is the first of the Chaar Sahibzade, the four sons of the Guru whom every Sikh remembers in Ardas.

## A youth at Anandpur Sahib

Ajit Singh Ji grew up at Anandpur Sahib, trained in horsemanship, swordsmanship and archery alongside the study of Gurmukhi and the bani. Tradition remembers him as tall, brave and calm. When he was about twelve the Khalsa was created, and he took Amrit with his family. In 1700, still a teenager, he was sent at the head of a band of Singhs to the village of Nuh, where a group of Ranghars had robbed a sangat on its way to Anandpur Sahib, and he returned having recovered what was taken.

## The defence of Anandpur

Through the long sieges of Anandpur Sahib by the hill rajas and the Mughal forces, Baba Ajit Singh Ji fought in its defence. When the Guru's household left the fort in December 1704, he rode with his father and his younger brother, Baba Jujhar Singh Ji.

## Chamkaur

At Chamkaur, besieged in a mud fortress by a vast army, he asked his father's permission to go out and fight, and the Guru armed him himself. He fell fighting, aged about eighteen. His younger brother followed him into battle the same day. Read the story of the Saka of Chamkaur Sahib.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark his birth anniversary with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Chamkaur Sahib and Anandpur Sahib, and young Sikhs often take part in gatka and kirtan in his memory.
label: Birth anniversary
imageCaption: Chamkaur Sahib, where Baba Ajit Singh Ji gave his life

title: Birth anniversary – Sahibzada Baba Jujhar Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sahibzada Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, second son of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, born at Anandpur Sahib in 1691, who fell at Chamkaur aged about fourteen.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Sahibzada Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, the second son of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, born at Anandpur Sahib in 1691 to Mata Jito Ji. He is remembered as one of the Vadde Sahibzade, the two elder sons of the Guru, who gave their lives at Chamkaur.

## Growing up at Anandpur Sahib

Jujhar Singh Ji grew up at Anandpur Sahib with his elder brother, Ajit Singh Ji, and his younger brothers, Zorawar Singh Ji and Fateh Singh Ji. Like them, he learned to ride and fight as well as to read the bani, and he took Amrit as a child. His name means one who fights to the last, and tradition remembers that he lived up to it.

## Chamkaur

When the Guru's family left Anandpur Sahib in December 1704, Jujhar Singh Ji rode with his father and elder brother to Chamkaur. There, in a mud fortress besieged by a far larger army, he watched his brother go out to fight and fall. He then asked his father for permission to follow. Tradition remembers that the Guru embraced him, armed him and sent him out with a small group of Singhs, and that the boy, about fourteen years old, fought his way into the enemy ranks before he fell. The Guru is remembered as watching from the garhi and giving thanks that his sons had been accepted in the Divine court. Read the story of the Saka of Chamkaur Sahib.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark the day with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Chamkaur Sahib and Anandpur Sahib. For children in Sikh families, the Sahibzade are among the first heroes they hear about, and the day is often marked with children's kirtan and stories.
label: Birth anniversary
imageCaption: Gurdwara Damdama Sahib, Chamkaur Sahib

title: Birth anniversary – Sahibzada Baba Zorawar Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sahibzada Baba Zorawar Singh Ji, born at Anandpur Sahib in 1696, who at nine refused to give up his faith in the court of Sirhind.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Sahibzada Baba Zorawar Singh Ji, the third son of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, born at Anandpur Sahib in 1696 to Mata Jito Ji. With his younger brother, Baba Fateh Singh Ji, he is remembered as one of the Chhote Sahibzade, the younger sons of the Guru.

## A childhood at Anandpur Sahib

Zorawar Singh Ji grew up at Anandpur Sahib in the years when the Khalsa was created and the town was repeatedly besieged. He was raised largely by his grandmother, Mata Gujri Ji, who taught the children the bani and the story of their grandfather, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, who had given his life in Delhi for the freedom of others.

## Steadfast at nine

When the family was scattered at the flooded Sirsa river in December 1704, Zorawar Singh Ji, Fateh Singh Ji and Mata Gujri Ji were separated from the Guru. Betrayed by their former cook, Gangu, they were taken to Sirhind and held in the cold Thanda Burj. Brought before the governor, Wazir Khan, the two boys were promised wealth and honour if they would give up their faith, and threatened with death if they would not. Tradition remembers Zorawar Singh Ji, as the elder, answering for both that they were the grandsons of Guru Tegh Bahadur and would not abandon their faith. They were bricked into a wall and put to death. Read the story of the Saka of Sirhind.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark his birth anniversary with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Anandpur Sahib and Fatehgarh Sahib, and many gurdwaras hold children's programmes telling the story of the Sahibzade.
label: Birth anniversary
imageCaption: Fatehgarh Sahib seen from the Thanda Burj, where the younger Sahibzade were held

title: Birth anniversary – Sahibzada Baba Fateh Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Sahibzada Baba Fateh Singh Ji, born at Anandpur Sahib in 1699, the youngest of the Chaar Sahibzade, martyred at Sirhind at six years old.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Sahibzada Baba Fateh Singh Ji, the youngest son of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, born at Anandpur Sahib in 1699, the year the Khalsa was created, to Mata Jito Ji. He was the youngest of the Chaar Sahibzade, and the town of Fatehgarh Sahib is named after him.

## The youngest of the four

Fateh Singh Ji spent his short childhood at Anandpur Sahib. Paintings and stories often show him in the blue dress and tall dumalla of a Nihang Singh, a small boy carrying the form of the Khalsa, and Nihang Singhs honour him as their own. He was raised with his brother Zorawar Singh Ji by their grandmother, Mata Gujri Ji.

## Sirhind

In December 1704, separated from the Guru at the Sirsa river and betrayed by Gangu, the two boys and their grandmother were held by Wazir Khan, the governor of Sirhind, in the Thanda Burj, a tower open to the winter wind. In court they refused every offer to give up their faith. Tradition remembers that they bowed to no one, entering with the greeting of the Khalsa. Fateh Singh Ji, about six years old, and his brother were bricked into a wall and then put to death, and Mata Gujri Ji passed away on hearing the news. Read the story of the Saka of Sirhind.

## How he is remembered

In 2022 the Government of India named 26 December Veer Bal Diwas in memory of the younger Sahibzade. Sikhs remember them every day in Ardas, and mark this birth anniversary with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Fatehgarh Sahib and Anandpur Sahib, often with programmes for children.
label: Birth anniversary
imageCaption: The sarovar at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib, named after Baba Fateh Singh Ji

title: Birth anniversary – Bhai Daya Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhai Daya Singh Ji, the Sikh from Lahore who rose first when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji asked for a head on Vaisakhi 1699. His life of service.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhai Daya Singh Ji, the first of the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. On Vaisakhi in 1699, when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji stood before the sangat at Anandpur Sahib with a drawn sword and asked who would give his head, he was the first to rise.

## Daya Ram of Lahore

He was born Daya Ram in 1661 in Lahore, into a Khatri family devoted to the Gurus, and came to Anandpur Sahib as a young man to serve. Tradition remembers him as learned in Persian and Punjabi.

## Vaisakhi 1699

When the Guru asked for a head, a hush fell over the gathering. Daya Ram stood up and offered his. The Guru took him into a tent and came out with his sword dripping, asking for another; four more Sikhs came forward, each from a different caste and region. The Guru then brought all five out dressed alike, gave them Khande di Pahul, the Amrit prepared with a double-edged sword, and named them Singh, and then asked them to give him Amrit in turn. Daya Ram became Bhai Daya Singh, his name meaning compassion. Read more about Vaisakhi and the creation of the Khalsa.

## A life beside the Guru

Bhai Daya Singh Ji remained close to the Guru for the rest of his life. He was one of the three Singhs who left the garhi at Chamkaur with the Guru in December 1704, and tradition remembers that he carried the Guru's letter, the Zafarnama, to the emperor Aurangzeb in the Deccan. He went south with the Guru to Nanded, and is believed to have passed away at Abchal Nagar there, where a memorial to him and Bhai Dharam Singh Ji stands.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember him with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur Sahib.
label: Birth anniversary
imageCaption: Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur Sahib, where the Khalsa was created

title: Birth anniversary – Bhai Dharam Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhai Dharam Singh Ji, the farmer from Hastinapur who became the second of the Panj Pyare in 1699 and stayed with the Guru to the end.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhai Dharam Singh Ji, the second of the Panj Pyare, who rose at Anandpur Sahib on Vaisakhi in 1699 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji asked a second time for a head.

## Dharam Das of Hastinapur

He was born Dharam Das in 1666 at Hastinapur, near Meerut, in today's Uttar Pradesh, into a Jat farming family. He came to Anandpur Sahib as a young man and stayed to serve the Guru. His journey from the plains of the Ganga shows how far the Guru's message had already travelled.

## The second head

After Bhai Daya Singh Ji had been taken into the tent, the Guru came out again with his sword and asked for another Sikh ready to give his head. Dharam Das stood up. With Bhai Daya Singh Ji, Bhai Himmat Singh Ji, Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji and Bhai Sahib Singh Ji, he received Khande di Pahul and became one of the first five members of the Khalsa, taking the name Dharam Singh, his name meaning righteousness. Read more about Vaisakhi and the creation of the Khalsa.

## To the end

Bhai Dharam Singh Ji fought in the defence of Anandpur Sahib and was with the Guru through the hardest days that followed. He was one of the three Singhs who left the garhi at Chamkaur with the Guru in December 1704, and he travelled with him through the Malwa and on to the Deccan. Tradition holds that he passed away at Nanded, where he is remembered alongside Bhai Daya Singh Ji.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember him with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib and at Hastinapur, where a gurdwara stands in his memory.
label: Birth anniversary
imageCaption: Anandpur Sahib, where Bhai Dharam Singh Ji became one of the Panj Pyare

title: Birth anniversary – Bhai Himmat Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhai Himmat Singh Ji, born at Jagannath Puri, the third of the Panj Pyare, who gave his life at Chamkaur Sahib in December 1704.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhai Himmat Singh Ji, the third of the Panj Pyare. When Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji asked for a head for the third time on Vaisakhi in 1699, it was a water-carrier from the far east of India who stood up.

## Himmat Rai of Puri

He was born Himmat Rai in 1661 at Jagannath Puri, on the coast of Odisha, into a family of water-carriers, a caste of low standing in that society. He came to Anandpur Sahib as a young man and served there for years, carrying water for the langar and the sangat.

## The third head

When the Guru stepped out of the tent a third time with his sword and called for another Sikh, Himmat Rai rose. He received Khande di Pahul with the other four and took the name Himmat Singh, his name meaning courage. That the five came from Lahore, Hastinapur, Puri, Dwarka and Bidar, and from castes the old order ranked high and low, was itself part of the Guru's message: in the Khalsa, all are one. Read more about Vaisakhi and the creation of the Khalsa.

## Chamkaur

Bhai Himmat Singh Ji fought in the defence of Anandpur Sahib and rode with the Guru when the fort was left in December 1704. At Chamkaur he was among the Singhs who went out of the garhi to face the besieging army, and he fell there, with Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji and Bhai Sahib Singh Ji.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember him with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib and at Chamkaur Sahib. A gurdwara at Jagannath Puri, Gurdwara Bauli Math, is associated with Guru Nanak Dev Ji's visit there, and Sikhs of Odisha keep his memory with pride.

title: Birth anniversary – Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji, born at Dwarka in Gujarat, the fourth of the Panj Pyare in 1699, who fell at Chamkaur Sahib in December 1704.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji, the fourth of the Panj Pyare, who came forward at Anandpur Sahib on Vaisakhi in 1699 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji called for a fourth head.

## Mohkam Chand of Dwarka

He was born Mohkam Chand in 1663 at Dwarka, on the coast of Gujarat, into a family of washermen and calico printers, a caste of low standing. He came to Anandpur Sahib as a young man, learned the bani and martial skills, and stayed in the Guru's service.

## The fourth head

When the Guru stepped out again and asked for another Sikh ready to die, Mohkam Chand stood up. He received Khande di Pahul with the other four and took the name Mohkam Singh, his name meaning firm and steadfast. With the other Pyare, he then gave Amrit to the Guru himself, who asked to be received into the Khalsa as its member, not only its creator. Read more about Vaisakhi and the creation of the Khalsa.

## Chamkaur

Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji fought in the battles around Anandpur Sahib and was known as a skilled warrior. In December 1704 he rode with the Guru to Chamkaur, and he was among the Singhs who went out of the garhi in small groups to meet the besieging army. He fell there with Bhai Himmat Singh Ji and Bhai Sahib Singh Ji.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember him with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib and Chamkaur Sahib. Gurdwara Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji at Bet Dwarka, in Gujarat, stands at his birthplace and draws Sikh pilgrims from across India.

title: Birth anniversary – Bhai Sahib Singh Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhai Sahib Singh Ji, born at Bidar in Karnataka, the fifth of the Panj Pyare in 1699, who fell at Chamkaur Sahib in December 1704.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhai Sahib Singh Ji, the fifth of the Panj Pyare, who completed the first five of the Khalsa when he rose at Anandpur Sahib on Vaisakhi in 1699.

## Sahib Chand of Bidar

He was born Sahib Chand in 1662 at Bidar, in today's Karnataka, into a family of barbers. Bidar already had a Sikh connection: Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji is remembered as having visited it on his journey south, at the place now called Gurdwara Nanak Jhira Sahib, where a spring flows. Sahib Chand came north to Anandpur Sahib as a young man and served the Guru there.

## The fifth head

When the Guru came out a fifth time and called for one more head, Sahib Chand stood up. With the other four he received Khande di Pahul, the Amrit prepared in an iron bowl stirred with a double-edged sword as the Guru recited the banis, and took the name Sahib Singh. A barber, of all people, now kept his own hair uncut as one of the Khalsa. Read more about Vaisakhi and the creation of the Khalsa.

## Chamkaur

Bhai Sahib Singh Ji fought in the defence of Anandpur Sahib, and in December 1704 he rode with the Guru to Chamkaur. There, as the small band of Singhs went out of the garhi in groups to face the besieging army, he fell, with Bhai Himmat Singh Ji and Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember him with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib and Chamkaur Sahib, and at Gurdwara Nanak Jhira Sahib in Bidar, where his birthplace is honoured.

title: Birth anniversary – Mata Sahib Kaur Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Mata Sahib Kaur Ji, honoured as the Mother of the Khalsa: her life with Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and her leadership of the Panth after him.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Mata Sahib Kaur Ji, whom Sikhs honour as the Mother of the Khalsa. Every Sikh who takes Amrit is told that their spiritual father is Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, their mother Mata Sahib Kaur Ji, and their home Anandpur Sahib.

## Sahib Devan of Rohtas

She was born Sahib Devan in 1681 at Rohtas, in the Jhelum district of today's Pakistan, to a devout Sikh family. Her parents offered her in marriage to Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, and she came to Anandpur Sahib and lived in the Guru's household. Tradition holds that she had no children of her own and that the Guru told her the Khalsa would be her children.

## The sweetness in the Amrit

Sikh tradition remembers that on Vaisakhi in 1699, as the Guru prepared the first Amrit, stirring water in an iron bowl with a double-edged sword, Mata Sahib Kaur Ji came forward and added patashas, sugar crystals, to the water, so that the strength of the steel would be joined by sweetness. It is for this that she is honoured as the Mother of the Khalsa.

## Leading the Panth

She stayed beside the Guru through the hardest years and travelled with him to the Deccan. After his passing she lived in Delhi with Mata Sundari Ji, and the two Matas guided the Panth for decades, issuing hukamnamas to the sangats under their seals and keeping the community together in years of persecution. She passed away in Delhi in 1747, and Gurdwara Bala Sahib holds her memorial.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember her with kirtan and Ardas, and many gurdwaras hold programmes led by women of the sangat, honouring her place in the Panth.
label: Birth anniversary

title: Baba Budha Ji
summary: Baba Budha Ji served six Gurus, anointed five of them and was the first granthi of Sri Harmandir Sahib. His life, his birth anniversary and the Jorh Mela at Thatha.
body:
Baba Budha Ji is remembered three times in the Nanakshahi calendar: on his birth anniversary, and on the two days of the Jorh Mela at Gurdwara Bir Baba Budha Sahib, Thatha, near Amritsar. He lived through the time of six Gurus, and no other Sikh served the Guru's house for so long.

## The wise boy

He was born Bura in 1506 at Kathu Nangal, near Amritsar. Sikh tradition tells that as a boy herding cattle he met Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, brought him milk, and asked how to be free of the fear of death; the Guru said he spoke with the wisdom of an old man, a budha, and the name stayed with him.

## Servant of six Gurus

Baba Budha Ji applied the tilak of Guruship to five Gurus, from Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji to Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji. He oversaw the digging of the sarovar at Amritsar, and when Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji installed the Adi Granth at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604, he was appointed its first granthi. He taught the young Hargobind Sahib Ji, and tradition remembers that Mata Ganga Ji walked to his forest camp, at the place now called Bir Baba Budha Sahib, with food she had made by hand, to ask his blessing for a son.

## The Jorh Mela at Thatha

He passed away at Ramdas in 1631, and Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji himself performed his last rites. The Jorh Mela at Gurdwara Bir Baba Budha Sahib, Thatha, draws large sangats, many of them couples praying for children, with kirtan, katha, Ardas and langar. Gurdwaras everywhere also mark his birth anniversary.

title: Birth anniversary – Bhagat Dhanna Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhagat Dhanna Ji, the Jat farmer of Rajasthan whose devotion is honoured in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, where his shabads are included.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhagat Dhanna Ji, a farmer of the fifteenth century from Rajasthan, whose shabads are included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. He is one of the fifteen Bhagats whose bani stands beside that of the Gurus, a sign that the Guru's scripture belongs to all who love the Divine, whatever their caste or birth.

## The farmer of Dhuan

Bhagat Dhanna Ji was born in 1415 at Dhuan Kalan, near Tonk in Rajasthan, into a family of Jat farmers. He tilled the land all his life. Tradition holds that he was drawn to devotion by the example of the saints of his time and became a disciple of Swami Ramanand, the teacher also remembered for Bhagat Kabir Ji and Bhagat Ravidas Ji.

## The stone and the simple heart

A well-known story tells that as a boy, Dhanna saw a Brahmin worshipping an idol and begged for one of his own. The Brahmin gave him an ordinary stone to be rid of him. Dhanna offered it food with such simple love, refusing to eat until it ate, that the Divine appeared to him. Sikh teaching tells this story not to praise idol worship, which the Gurus rejected, but to show that what reaches the Divine is sincere love.

## His bani

The shabads of Bhagat Dhanna Ji are included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, in Raag Aasa and Raag Dhanasari. One of them, sung in the evening Arti, is a farmer's simple prayer for the needs of a household. Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, in his own bani, names Dhanna among the devotees who found the Divine through love.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark the day with kirtan of his shabads and with Ardas, and a gurdwara at Dhuan Kalan keeps his memory.
label: Birth anniversary

title: Birth anniversary – Bhagat Kabir Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhagat Kabir Ji, the weaver-poet of Varanasi whose bani is the largest of the Bhagats' in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. His life and teaching.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhagat Kabir Ji, the weaver-poet of Kashi, now Varanasi, whose bani has the largest place among the Bhagats in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Outside the Sikh tradition, the day is widely kept as Kabir Jayanti, on the full moon of Jeth.

## The weaver of Kashi

Kabir Ji lived in the fifteenth century and was raised in a family of Muslim weavers, the julahas, at Kashi, the holiest city of Hinduism. He worked at the loom all his life and never left the life of a householder. Tradition holds that he was a disciple of Swami Ramanand. He spoke against the pride of caste, the empty rituals of both Hindus and Muslims, and the claim of priests to stand between people and the Divine, and he paid for it with persecution.

## His bani

Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji included more than five hundred of Kabir Ji's shabads and shaloks in the Adi Granth, written in a plain, earthy language full of images from the loom, the market and the household. His bani speaks of devotion to the one Formless Creator, of death as a constant reminder, and of the Divine found within rather than in temples, mosques or pilgrimages.

## His last days

In old age, tradition says, Kabir Ji left Kashi for Maghar, a town believed to bring a bad rebirth to anyone who died there, to show that a person's fate depends on their devotion, not the place of death. A story very like the one told of Guru Nanak Dev Ji says that Hindus and Muslims disputed his body and found only flowers.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark the day with kirtan of his shabads and katha on his life, and the Kabir Chaura in Varanasi draws pilgrims of many faiths.
label: Birth anniversary

title: Birth anniversary – Bhagat Namdev Ji
summary: The birth anniversary of Bhagat Namdev Ji, the calico printer from Maharashtra whose sixty-one shabads are in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, and who spent his last years in Punjab.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhagat Namdev Ji, the saint-poet of Maharashtra whose bani is included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. He lived about two centuries before Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, and his life joins the devotional traditions of Maharashtra and Punjab.

## The calico printer

Namdev Ji was born in 1270 at Narsi Bamani, in today's Hingoli district of Maharashtra, into a family of tailors and calico printers, a caste of low standing. He grew up near Pandharpur, and from childhood was absorbed in devotion. Stories remember him being turned away from a temple because of his caste, and the temple itself turning to face him as he sang outside. Sikh teaching tells such stories to show that the Divine answers love, not birth.

## His bani

Sixty-one shabads of Bhagat Namdev Ji are included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, in eighteen raags. They speak of the One Divine present everywhere, reject caste and empty ritual, and are full of the warmth of a devotee who speaks to the Divine as a friend. Several are sung often in kirtan. The Gurus refer to him again and again as an example of a low-born devotee raised up by devotion.

## Ghuman

In his later years Namdev Ji travelled north and spent about twenty years in Punjab, at the village of Ghuman in Gurdaspur district, where he preached and is believed to have passed away in 1350. Gurdwara Bhagat Namdev Ji at Ghuman marks the place, and a mela is held there every year.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark the day with kirtan of his shabads and Ardas, above all at Ghuman, and at Pandharpur, where his memory is honoured by the Warkari tradition.
label: Birth anniversary
imageCaption: Gurdwara Bhagat Namdev Ji, Punjab

title: Birth anniversary – Bhagat Ravidas Ji (650th anniversary)
summary: The 650th birth anniversary of Bhagat Ravidas Ji, the cobbler-saint of Kashi whose forty shabads in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji speak of a city without sorrow, Begumpura.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Bhagat Ravidas Ji, the saint of Kashi whose bani is included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, and in Nanakshahi 558 the SGPC's calendar marks his 650th birth anniversary. Widely celebrated as Guru Ravidas Jayanti, the day falls on the full moon of Magh.

## The cobbler of Kashi

Ravidas Ji was born at Seer Goverdhanpur, near Kashi, now Varanasi, into a family of leather workers, a community the caste order treated as untouchable. He worked as a cobbler all his life, mending shoes and giving freely to holy men who came to him. Tradition holds that he was a disciple of Swami Ramanand and a contemporary of Bhagat Kabir Ji, and that Mirabai, the Rajput princess-poet, honoured him as her teacher.

## His bani

Forty shabads and one shalok of Bhagat Ravidas Ji are included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, in sixteen raags. He speaks openly of his caste and of those who despised it, and says that devotion has made him greater than those who looked down on him. His best-known shabad describes Begumpura, a city without sorrow, where there is no tax, no fear, no second or third class of person, a vision of a just society that still inspires.

## How he is remembered

For millions, above all in the Ravidassia community of Punjab, he is Guru Ravidas Ji. His birthplace at Seer Goverdhanpur draws vast crowds, and Nagar Kirtans are held in Punjab and around the world.

## How the day is observed

In gurdwaras, sangats mark the day with kirtan of his shabads, katha on his life and Ardas.
label: Birth anniversary

title: Birth anniversary – Sardar Jassa Singh Ramgarhia
summary: The birth anniversary of Sardar Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, leader of the Ramgarhia Misl, who rebuilt the fort of Ram Rauni at Amritsar and rode into Delhi in 1783.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Sardar Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, one of the great leaders of the Khalsa in the eighteenth century and the head of the Ramgarhia Misl, whose twin towers still stand beside Sri Harmandir Sahib.

## Early life

Jassa Singh was born in 1723 at Ichogil, near Lahore, into a family of carpenters, the son of Giani Bhagwan Singh. He grew up in the years when the Mughal governors of Lahore hunted the Sikhs, and joined the Khalsa as a young man, fighting under Nawab Kapur Singh.

## Ram Rauni

In 1748 the Khalsa built a mud fort near Amritsar called Ram Rauni, after Sri Guru Ram Das Ji, and were besieged in it. Jassa Singh, then serving with the Mughal side, changed sides and helped the besieged Sikhs. He later rebuilt the fort, renamed it Ramgarh, and took charge of it, and from it he and his followers took the name Ramgarhia. His misl came to hold lands around Batala and in the hills.

## Delhi and the Bunga

In 1783 he rode with Sardar Baghel Singh and Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia into Delhi, and tradition remembers that he carried back to Amritsar a slab of stone from the Mughal court, which is kept at the Ramgarhia Bunga. The Bunga, a fortified residence with two tall towers in the Sri Harmandir Sahib complex, was built by his misl to guard the shrine. He passed away in 1803.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember him with kirtan and Ardas, and the Ramgarhia community holds gatherings in his memory in Punjab and around the world.

title: Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia
summary: Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia led the Dal Khalsa, freed Sikh captives from Abdali's army and laid the new foundation of Sri Harmandir Sahib. His birth anniversary and passing.
body:
Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia is remembered twice in the Nanakshahi calendar, at his birth anniversary in spring and on the anniversary of his passing in autumn. He was the foremost leader of the Khalsa in the mid-eighteenth century, honoured by the Sikhs as Sultan-ul-Qaum, king of the nation.

## Raised by Mata Sundari Ji

Jassa Singh was born in 1718 at Ahlu, near Lahore, and lost his father when he was four. His mother took him to Delhi, where he spent several years in the household of Mata Sundari Ji, the widow of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, learning the bani and the kirtan of the Asa di Vaar. He was then entrusted to Nawab Kapur Singh, who raised him as a warrior and leader.

## The Dal Khalsa

In 1748, at Amritsar, the Sarbat Khalsa united the Sikh bands into the Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa, under his command, and he led the Ahluwalia Misl. In 1761 his forces fell on Ahmad Shah Abdali's army as it returned from Panipat and freed more than two thousand captive women, who were returned to their homes. He was wounded many times shielding the caravan at the Wadda Ghallughara of 1762. In 1764, after Abdali had blown up Sri Harmandir Sahib, he laid the foundation of its reconstruction. In 1783 he rode with Sardar Baghel Singh and Sardar Jassa Singh Ramgarhia into Delhi.

## His passing

He passed away at Amritsar in 1783, and his samadh stands near Gurdwara Baba Atal Rai. His misl later became the ruling family of Kapurthala.

## How he is remembered

Sangats remember him with kirtan and Ardas on both days, and katha recalls a leader who stayed devoted to the bani all his life.

title: Birth anniversary – Sant Giani Kartar Singh Ji Bhindranwale
summary: The birth anniversary of Sant Giani Kartar Singh Ji Bhindranwale, head of the Damdami Taksal from 1969 to 1977, remembered for his katha and for teaching Gurbani pronunciation.
body:
This day celebrates the birth of Sant Giani Kartar Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale, who led the Damdami Taksal, a seminary of Sikh learning, from 1969 until his death in 1977. He is remembered above all as a teacher of the Guru's bani, its correct pronunciation and its meaning.

## The Damdami Taksal

The Damdami Taksal traces its tradition to Damdama Sahib, where Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji had Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji written out in 1706 and, by tradition, taught its meaning to a group of Sikhs led by Baba Deep Singh Ji. Over the centuries the Taksal, which takes its name from a mint, became known for training granthis, kathavachaks and kirtanis in santhiya, the careful study of how each word of the bani is pronounced and understood. In the twentieth century it was led by Sant Sunder Singh Ji Bhindranwale and then Sant Gurbachan Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale, the name coming from the village of Bhinder Kalan.

## A life of teaching

Kartar Singh Ji was born in 1932 at Bhure Kohna, near Amritsar, and studied under Sant Gurbachan Singh Ji, becoming one of his leading students. As head of the Taksal he travelled widely, giving katha of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and of the Sikh histories, and many of his recorded katha sessions are still listened to today. He encouraged Sikhs to take Amrit and to keep the rehat, and trained many students in santhiya. He set up the Taksal's headquarters at Gurdwara Gurdarshan Parkash at Mehta Chowk.

## His passing

He died in a road accident in 1977, and was succeeded by Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale.

## How the day is observed

The day is observed with Akhand Paath, kirtan and katha, especially at Mehta Chowk.

title: Foundation Stone of Sachkhand Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar
summary: How the foundation of Sri Harmandir Sahib was laid in the sarovar at Amritsar in 1588, the part of Sai Mian Mir, and why the temple has four doors and sits low.
body:
This day remembers the laying of the foundation of Sachkhand Sri Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple, in the middle of the sarovar at Amritsar, at the end of the 1580s. The SGPC's calendar for Nanakshahi 558 lists the anniversary on two dates, one in summer and one at the start of the month of Magh, the date most often given by tradition.

## A temple in the pool

Sri Guru Ram Das Ji had founded the town of Ramdaspur and dug the sarovar, the pool of nectar that gave Amritsar its name. His son, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, completed the pool and resolved to build a house of the Guru in its centre. Tradition remembers that he invited his friend, the Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir of Lahore, to lay the foundation stone, a gesture of the respect the Gurus gave to people of every faith. Baba Budha Ji, Bhai Gurdas Ji and the sangat took part, and the building was completed in 1604, when the Adi Granth was installed in it.

## Built to be open

The Guru made choices that still speak. Sri Harmandir Sahib was set lower than the ground around it, so that every visitor walks down to it in humility. It was given four doors, one on each side, as a sign that it is open to people of every caste, creed and direction. The walkway across the water joins it to the Darshani Deori, the gateway.

## The temple through history

The temple was attacked and destroyed several times in the eighteenth century, and each time the Khalsa rebuilt it, the present building from 1764. In the early nineteenth century Maharaja Ranjit Singh covered its upper floors in gilded copper, which gave it the name the Golden Temple.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Sri Harmandir Sahib for kirtan and Ardas, and many bathe in the sarovar.

title: Foundation Stone / Sirjana Divas – Sri Akal Takht Sahib
summary: In 1606 Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji built the Akal Bunga facing Sri Harmandir Sahib. The story of Sri Akal Takht Sahib, its role in the Panth, and how its Sirjana Divas is kept.
body:
The Sirjana Divas of Sri Akal Takht Sahib remembers the founding in 1606 of the Throne of the Timeless, facing Sri Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. It is the first and highest of the five Takhts, the seats of authority of the Sikh Panth.

## The Akal Bunga

After the shaheedi of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the young Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji built a raised platform across the courtyard from Sri Harmandir Sahib. Tradition remembers that Baba Budha Ji and Bhai Gurdas Ji built it with their own hands, with no mason allowed to touch it but the Guru and his Sikhs. It was raised higher than the throne of any emperor, about twelve feet, a statement that the Sikhs answered to the Timeless One alone. It was called the Akal Bunga.

## Miri beside Piri

From the Akal Bunga the Guru held court, received the sangat, heard disputes and issued his commands, while Sri Harmandir Sahib remained the place of the Word and of kirtan. He watched wrestling and martial exercises in the courtyard, and in the evening ballads of heroism were sung there, the beginning of the dhadi tradition. The two buildings, facing each other, are a picture of Miri and Piri together.

## The voice of the Panth

In the eighteenth century the Sarbat Khalsa gathered at Sri Akal Takht Sahib to take decisions as the Guru Panth, and it remains the place from which hukamnamas to the whole Panth are issued. The building has been destroyed and rebuilt several times, most recently after June 1984.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, and the Jathedar addresses the Panth.
