title: Sampuranta Divas – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Sri Harmandir Sahib
summary: Sampuranta Divas remembers the completion of the Adi Granth by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Bhai Gurdas Ji at Ramsar, Amritsar, in 1604, days before its first installation.
body:
Sampuranta Divas remembers the completion in 1604 of the Adi Granth, the scripture that became Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Sampuranta means completeness. The day comes shortly before the Pehla Prakash Purab, when the finished Granth was installed at Sri Harmandir Sahib.

## Ramsar

To compile the Granth, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji withdrew to a quiet place outside Amritsar, beside a pool now called Ramsar, and worked there for about a year. Gurdwara Ramsar Sahib marks the place. The Guru gathered the bani of the first four Gurus, much of it from the pothis kept at Goindwal by the family of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, which Baba Mohan Ji, the third Guru's son, was persuaded to give. He added his own bani, and the compositions of fifteen Bhagats, among them Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sheikh Farid, and of Bhatts and Sikhs of the Guru's court.

## Written by Bhai Gurdas Ji

The Guru dictated and Bhai Gurdas Ji, the learned Sikh who was also the Guru's maternal uncle, wrote it out. The bani was arranged with great care, by raag, the musical measure in which it is sung, and within each raag by author and form. At its head stands the Mool Mantar and Japji Sahib.

## Completion and installation

When the work was finished, it was carried in procession to Sri Harmandir Sahib and installed, with Baba Budha Ji as the first granthi. A century later, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji added the bani of the ninth Guru and gave the Granth the Guruship. Read about the Pehla Prakash Purab.

## How the day is observed

Sangats hold kirtan and Ardas at Sri Harmandir Sahib and Gurdwara Ramsar Sahib.
label: Day in history

title: Marriage Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji & Mata Jito Ji
summary: In 1677 Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji married Mata Jito Ji at a village near Anandpur Sahib that came to be called Guru Ka Lahore. The story and the Basant Panchmi mela.
body:
This day remembers the marriage in 1677 of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and Mata Jito Ji, at a place in the hills near Anandpur Sahib that has been known ever since as Guru Ka Lahore. It is celebrated on Basant Panchmi with a mela at Guru Ka Lahore, in the Bilaspur district of Himachal Pradesh.

## Why Guru Ka Lahore

Mata Jito Ji was the daughter of Bhai Hari Jas, a Sikh of Lahore. Her family wished the wedding to be held in Lahore with the Guru's procession coming to them. But the Guru, then a young man of about eleven, could not travel there in safety, since the Mughal authorities were hostile after the shaheedi of his father, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji. So the Guru's family arranged for a small town to be laid out in the hills a few miles north of Anandpur Sahib, and named it Lahore, so that the bride's family could say the wedding had taken place at Lahore. It is remembered as Guru Ka Lahore, the Guru's Lahore.

## The springs of Guru Ka Lahore

Tradition remembers that there was no water at the place, and that the Guru struck the ground with his spear and his arrow, and springs came out that still flow, called Tir Ganga and Paatal Ganga.

## Mata Jito Ji

Mata Jito Ji was the mother of three of the Chaar Sahibzade: Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji. She lived at Anandpur Sahib, where she passed away in 1700, and Gurdwara Mata Jito Ji at Agampur, near Anandpur Sahib, keeps her memory.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Gurdwara Guru Ka Lahore on Basant Panchmi for kirtan, Ardas and langar.
label: Day in history

title: Basant Panchmi
summary: What Basant Panchmi means in the Sikh tradition: the season of Raag Basant at Sri Harmandir Sahib, the mela at Chheharta Sahib, and the Guru's marriage at Guru Ka Lahore.
body:
Basant Panchmi, the fifth day of the bright half of the month of Magh, is the festival of spring across North India, when the fields of Punjab turn yellow with mustard flowers. In the Sikh tradition it is a day of several memories, and the SGPC's calendar keeps it as a day in Sikh history.

## Raag Basant

Raag Basant, the raag of spring, is one of the thirty-one raags of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, with bani by the Gurus and the Bhagats. The Gurus used the images of spring, of fresh growth and blossoming, to speak of the soul that blossoms when it remembers the Divine, rather than of outward festivity. At Sri Harmandir Sahib, by long tradition, kirtan in Raag Basant is sung through the season, beginning around Maghi and continuing until Hola Mohalla.

## Chheharta Sahib

At Chheharta, near Amritsar, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji had a large well dug for the villages around, worked by six Persian wheels, the chhe harte that gave the place its name. Gurdwara Chheharta Sahib marks the place, and a large mela is held there on Basant Panchmi, when sangats come for kirtan and to drink from the well.

## Guru Ka Lahore

Basant Panchmi is also the day on which Sikhs remember the marriage of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and Mata Jito Ji at Guru Ka Lahore, near Anandpur Sahib, where a mela is held. Read about the marriage at Guru Ka Lahore.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras hold kirtan in Raag Basant, and many Sikhs wear yellow, the colour of the season and of the mustard fields.
label: Day in history

title: Victory at Sirhind – Banda Singh Bahadur & Baba Deep Singh
summary: On 12 May 1710 the Khalsa under Baba Banda Singh Bahadur defeated Wazir Khan at Chappar Chiri and took Sirhind, where the younger Sahibzade had been martyred. The story.
body:
This day remembers the battle of Chappar Chiri on 12 May 1710, in which the Khalsa led by Baba Banda Singh Bahadur defeated the army of Wazir Khan, the governor of Sirhind, and went on to take the city. For the Sikhs it was the answer to the martyrdom of the younger Sahibzade at Sirhind six years before.

## The road to Sirhind

Sent to Punjab by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1708, Banda Singh Bahadur gathered the Khalsa and took Samana, Sadhaura and other towns. Sikhs from across Punjab joined him, many from the Majha crossing the Sutlej to reach him. Wazir Khan, who had ordered the death of Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, raised a large army with artillery and elephants, and called for a holy war against the Sikhs.

## Chappar Chiri

The armies met on the plain of Chappar Chiri, about twenty kilometres from Sirhind. The Khalsa was outnumbered and lacked guns, and the early fighting went hard. Banda Singh Bahadur himself led a charge into the centre of the enemy line, and the Sikhs broke it. Wazir Khan was killed in the battle. Some accounts hold that Baba Deep Singh Ji fought there too, which is why the SGPC's calendar names both leaders. Two days later the Khalsa entered Sirhind.

## After the victory

Banda Singh Bahadur appointed a Sikh governor of Sirhind, set up his capital at Lohgarh and struck coins in the name of the Gurus. The Fateh Burj, the tower of victory, now stands at Chappar Chiri.

## How the day is observed

Sangats mark the day with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Chappar Chiri and Fatehgarh Sahib.
label: Day in history
imageCaption: The Fateh Burj at Chappar Chiri, built in 2011 to remember the victory

title: Chhota Ghallughara – Kahnuwan (Gurdaspur)
summary: In 1746 the forces of Lahore under Lakhpat Rai trapped thousands of Sikhs in the marshes of Kahnuwan. About seven thousand were killed and three thousand executed in Lahore.
body:
The Chhota Ghallughara, the lesser holocaust, was a massacre of Sikhs in the spring of 1746 in the marshy forests around Kahnuwan, near Gurdaspur, carried out by the forces of the Mughal administration of Lahore. Sikh sources say about seven thousand were killed in the fighting and three thousand more taken prisoner and executed in Lahore.

## Lakhpat Rai's revenge

In those years the Sikhs lived as fugitives in the forests and hills, with a price on their heads. In early 1746 a band of Sikhs killed Jaspat Rai, the faujdar of Eminabad, in a skirmish. His brother, Lakhpat Rai, a powerful minister at the court of Yahiya Khan, the governor of Lahore, swore to wipe out the Sikhs. He had Sikhs living in Lahore rounded up and executed, banned the reading of Gurmukhi, and ordered the destruction of Sikh places.

## The marshes of Kahnuwan

He then marched out with a large army, cannon and local levies. About fifteen thousand Sikhs, among them many families, took refuge in the swampy forests of Kahnuwan near the Ravi. The army surrounded the area and burned the forest. Trapped between the soldiers, the swamp, the river and the hills, where the hill rajas refused them shelter, the Sikhs fought their way out over several days, suffering terrible losses. The leaders who survived, among them Nawab Kapur Singh and Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, broke through and reached the Malwa.

## How it is remembered

The prisoners were taken to Lahore and executed at the Nakhas, where Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj stands. Within two years the Khalsa had regrouped into the Dal Khalsa. Sikhs remember the shaheeds with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, and at a memorial near Kahnuwan.
label: Day in history

title: Leaving of Sri Anandpur Sahib Fort
summary: After a siege of months, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji left Anandpur Sahib on the night of 20 December 1704 on promises of safe passage that were broken within hours. The story.
body:
This day remembers the night in December 1704 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, his family and the Sikhs left the fort of Anandpur Sahib after a long siege. It begins the Shaheedi week of December, the most sorrowful days of the Sikh year, in which the Guru lost his mother and all four of his sons.

## The siege

The hill rajas had long resented the Guru's growing power and his Khalsa, which rejected caste and gave ordinary people dignity and arms. With the forces of the Mughal governors of Sirhind and Lahore, they besieged Anandpur Sahib through 1704. Food ran out; the Sikhs ate leaves and bark. Some Sikhs, worn down, signed a disclaimer saying they were no longer the Guru's Sikhs and left; they would return at Muktsar.

## The oaths

The besiegers sent promises of safe passage if the Guru would leave the fort. The rajas swore on the cow and the Mughal commanders on the Quran, and a letter was brought said to carry the emperor Aurangzeb's own oath. The Guru doubted them, and tradition remembers that he tested them by sending out bullocks loaded with rubbish, which the besiegers fell upon. In the end, at the pleading of the sangat and of his mother, Mata Gujri Ji, he agreed to go.

## The night of leaving

On the night of 20 December, in the cold and rain, the Guru, the Sahibzade, Mata Gujri Ji, Mata Sundari Ji, Mata Sahib Kaur Ji and the Sikhs left the fort. Within hours the oaths were broken and the army fell on them as they reached the Sirsa river. Read on: the separation at the Sirsa river.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas, and many Sikhs begin the week of remembrance.
label: Day in history
imageCaption: Anandpur Sahib, the town of the Khalsa

title: Family separation at Sirsa River
summary: On the night after leaving Anandpur Sahib in December 1704, the Guru's family was scattered at the flooded Sirsa river. What happened at Parivar Vichhora, and what followed.
body:
Parivar Vichhora, the separation of the family, remembers what happened on the bank of the Sirsa river in December 1704, a few hours after Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji left Anandpur Sahib. In the dark and the flood, the Guru's family was scattered, and most of them never saw each other again.

## The attack at the river

The oaths of safe passage were broken almost at once. As the Guru's party reached the Sirsa, a stream swollen into a torrent by winter rain, the besieging armies attacked. Many Sikhs held back the attackers so that the others could cross, and many were swept away in the current. Precious manuscripts, among them much of the Guru's own writing, were lost in the water. Tradition remembers that the Guru held the morning Asa di Vaar kirtan on the bank even as the battle went on.

## Three ways

In the confusion the family was split into three. The Guru, his two elder sons, Baba Ajit Singh Ji and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, and about forty Singhs crossed and rode towards Chamkaur. Mata Gujri Ji and the two youngest, Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, were carried downstream and taken in by their former cook, Gangu, who betrayed them at Sirhind. Mata Sundari Ji and Mata Sahib Kaur Ji were escorted to Delhi by Bhai Mani Singh Ji. Within a week the elder sons fell at Chamkaur and the younger were martyred at Sirhind.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwara Parivar Vichhora stands on the bank of the Sirsa, near Ropar, and sangats gather there for kirtan and Ardas. Read on: the Saka of Chamkaur Sahib and the Saka of Sirhind.
label: Day in history
imageCaption: Gurdwara Parivar Vichhora, on the bank of the Sirsa

title: Darbar Khalsa (Dussehra)
summary: Why the SGPC's calendar marks Dussehra as Darbar Khalsa: the Khalsa's gatherings, the shastar tradition at Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, and the Sikh view of the festival.
body:
The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar marks Dussehra as Darbar Khalsa, a day when the Khalsa gathers in darbar. While Dussehra is a Hindu festival celebrating the victory of Rama over Ravana, in the Sikh tradition the day is kept in its own way, as a gathering of the Khalsa and an occasion to honour the shastar, the weapons that the Gurus gave the Khalsa to defend the weak.

## The Khalsa in darbar

In the eighteenth century, when the Khalsa lived as fugitives and fought for survival, its bands came together at set times of the year to meet, to take decisions as the Sarbat Khalsa and to plan. Vaisakhi and Diwali at Amritsar were the best known of these gatherings. Festival days, when people were on the move in any case, allowed the scattered jathas to meet. A darbar of the Khalsa on such a day is a reminder of a community that governed itself in the presence of the Guru.

## The tradition at Hazur Sahib

At Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib in Nanded, where Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji spent his last days, Dussehra is kept with a great procession in which the Takht's historic weapons are carried out and displayed, and the Nihang Singhs and sangat take part. Many Nihang Singh dals hold their own gatherings and displays of gatka on the day.

## A Sikh reading of the day

The Gurus taught that victory over evil begins with victory over the five thieves within: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Katha on the day often turns to this inner meaning.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan, katha and Ardas, and in some places the shastar are honoured.
label: Day in history

title: Morcha Guru Ka Bagh, Amritsar
summary: In 1922 Sikh jathas went day after day to cut firewood at Guru Ka Bagh, near Amritsar, and were beaten by police without striking back. The story of the morcha.
body:
The Morcha Guru Ka Bagh was a non-violent campaign in 1922 at Gurdwara Guru Ka Bagh, about twenty kilometres from Amritsar, during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. For weeks, jathas of Sikhs walked to the gurdwara and were beaten by the police without lifting a hand in return, and their courage moved people across India and abroad.

## Firewood for the langar

Guru Ka Bagh, at the village of Ghukewali, is associated with visits by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji. Like many shrines, it had been in the hands of a mahant, who had agreed to hand it to the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. But when Sikhs cut firewood for the langar from the trees on the gurdwara's land, as they always had, the mahant complained of theft, and in August 1922 the police arrested five Sikhs.

## Jatha after jatha

The SGPC began sending jathas each day to cut wood, each member pledged to non-violence. At the bridge near the gurdwara the police beat them with lathis until they fell, day after day. Hundreds were injured and thousands arrested. The Rev. C. F. Andrews, a friend of Gandhi, came to watch and wrote that he had seen a new heroism, and that the Sikhs had learned the lesson of the cross. Even a jatha of retired soldiers, many decorated in the First World War, took the blows.

## The outcome

Under public pressure, the beatings stopped in September, and in November the land was bought by a sympathiser and handed over. The morcha strengthened the movement that led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember it with kirtan and Ardas at Guru Ka Bagh and elsewhere.
label: Day in history

title: Chabiyan Da Morcha, Amritsar
summary: In 1921 the British seized the keys of the Toshakhana of Sri Harmandir Sahib. The Sikhs' non-violent Morcha of the Keys won them back on 19 January 1922. The story.
body:
Chabiyan Da Morcha, the Morcha of the Keys, was a non-violent campaign in 1921 and 1922 to recover the keys of the Toshakhana, the treasury of Sri Harmandir Sahib, from the British authorities. Its success on 19 January 1922 was the first great victory of the Gurdwara Reform Movement.

## The keys

Under British rule, the management of Sri Harmandir Sahib was in the hands of a manager, the sarbrah, appointed by the government. In 1920 the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee was formed to bring the gurdwaras under the Panth's own care, and in October 1921 it asked the sarbrah to hand over the keys of the Toshakhana, which holds the shrine's treasures. Instead, the Deputy Commissioner of Amritsar sent an official to collect the keys from him.

## The morcha

The SGPC declared that the Sikhs would not accept government control of their gurdwara. Meetings were held across Punjab, and Sikhs began wearing black turbans in protest and refusing to cooperate. Many leaders, among them Baba Kharak Singh, the president of the SGPC, were arrested, and hundreds of Sikhs courted arrest. The movement stayed non-violent throughout.

## The keys returned

Faced with mass protest, the government released the prisoners and, on 19 January 1922, sent an official to hand the keys to Baba Kharak Singh at a large gathering at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. Mahatma Gandhi sent a telegram calling it the first decisive battle for India's freedom won.

## How the day is observed

Sangats remember it with Ardas at Sri Akal Takht Sahib and with katha about the reform movement.
label: Day in history
imageCaption: The square in front of Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, about 1924

title: Jaito Da Morcha / Mela, Faridkot
summary: In 1923 an Akhand Paath at Gurdwara Gangsar, Jaito, was broken off by the authorities. The morcha that followed, the firing on the shaheedi jatha in February 1924, and the mela.
body:
Jaito Da Morcha was a long non-violent campaign of 1923 to 1925 at Jaito, in today's Faridkot district, during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. It is remembered each year with a mela at Jaito, on the anniversary of the firing on the shaheedi jatha in February 1924.

## The interrupted Akhand Paath

In 1923 the British forced Maharaja Ripudaman Singh of Nabha, who sympathised with the Akali movement, to give up his throne. Sikhs gathered at Gurdwara Gangsar Sahib in Jaito, a town then in Nabha state, to hold an Akhand Paath and pray for his restoration. In September 1923 the police arrested the sangat and broke off the reading before it was complete. For Sikhs, interrupting an Akhand Paath was an intolerable insult to the Guru.

## The jathas

The SGPC began sending jathas to Jaito to complete the Akhand Paath. Each was arrested. On 21 February 1924, a shaheedi jatha of five hundred Sikhs, followed by thousands of sympathisers, reached Gurdwara Tibbi Sahib near Jaito. The state forces opened fire. Many were killed and many more wounded. The jathas kept coming, from Punjab and from Sikh communities as far away as Canada and Shanghai.

## The outcome

The morcha ended in 1925 with the passing of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act. The authorities allowed the Akhand Paath to be completed at Gangsar, and in August 1925 one hundred and one Akhand Paaths were held there together.

## How the day is observed

A mela is held at Jaito on the anniversary, with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas at Gurdwara Gangsar Sahib and Gurdwara Tibbi Sahib.
label: Day in history
imageCaption: Gurdwara Gangsar Sahib, Jaito, where the morcha began

title: Sardar Baghel Singh – conquest of Delhi
summary: In March 1783 Sardar Baghel Singh led the Khalsa into Delhi and stayed to build seven gurdwaras at the places of the Gurus, among them Sis Ganj, Rakab Ganj and Bangla Sahib.
body:
This day remembers March 1783, when the Khalsa under Sardar Baghel Singh entered Delhi and raised the Nishan Sahib over the Red Fort. The SGPC's calendar keeps the anniversary on a fixed solar date. Its lasting legacy is the gurdwaras of Delhi, which Baghel Singh built at the places linked to the Gurus.

## Sardar Baghel Singh

Baghel Singh was born in the 1730s near Amritsar and rose to lead the Karorsinghia Misl, with lands in the Doaba and around Chhalaudi. In the 1770s and 1780s the misls made repeated expeditions across the Yamuna into the lands around Delhi, where the Mughal empire had grown weak.

## Into Delhi

In March 1783 Baghel Singh, with Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Sardar Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, led a large Khalsa force into Delhi. Their camp outside the city, where thirty thousand horsemen were gathered, is remembered in the name of the area Tis Hazari. The Khalsa entered the Red Fort, and the emperor Shah Alam II came to terms with them.

## The gurdwaras of Delhi

Baghel Singh agreed to withdraw most of his men on condition that he could stay with a small force to find and mark the places linked to the Gurus, and receive part of the city's revenue to build them. With the help of local people, he identified seven places, and built gurdwaras at them: Mata Sundari Ji, Bangla Sahib, Rakab Ganj, Sis Ganj, Moti Bagh, Majnu Ka Tilla and Bala Sahib. Many of Delhi's best-known gurdwaras stand on his foundations.

## How the day is observed

Delhi's sangat celebrates the day as Fateh Divas with kirtan, Ardas and Nagar Kirtan.
label: Day in history
imageCaption: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib, Delhi, about 1915, first built by Sardar Baghel Singh in 1783

title: Khalsa Saajna Divas / Vaisakhi – Creation of Khalsa Panth
summary: Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur Sahib: Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji asks for a head, the Panj Pyare, Khande di Pahul and the five Ks. The story of Khalsa Saajna Divas and its celebration.
body:
Vaisakhi is the harvest festival of Punjab, but for Sikhs it is above all Khalsa Saajna Divas, the day in 1699 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji created the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib. It is one of the most important days of the Sikh year, celebrated by Sikhs across the world.

## A sword and a question

The Guru called Sikhs from far and wide to Anandpur Sahib for Vaisakhi, and a vast sangat gathered on the hill where Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib now stands. The Guru came out with a drawn sword and asked who would give his head for the faith. A silence fell. Then Daya Ram of Lahore stood up. The Guru took him into a tent and came out with his sword dripping, asking for another. One by one, Dharam Das, Himmat Rai, Mohkam Chand and Sahib Chand came forward, from different castes and corners of India.

## The Panj Pyare and the Amrit

The Guru brought all five out, dressed alike, and called them the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. He prepared Amrit in an iron bowl, stirring water with a double-edged sword, the khanda, while reciting the banis, and Mata Sahib Kaur Ji added sugar crystals. He gave them Khande di Pahul, named each of them Singh, gave them the five Ks, the articles of faith beginning with kes, the uncut hair, and a code of discipline. Then he knelt before them and asked them to give Amrit to him, joining the Khalsa he had created.

## How Vaisakhi is celebrated

Sikhs mark the day with Akhand Paath, Nagar Kirtans led by five Singhs dressed as the Panj Pyare, Amrit Sanchar ceremonies, kirtan and langar. The Nishan Sahib at many gurdwaras is taken down, washed and given a new cloth. The largest gatherings are at Anandpur Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo, and at Sri Harmandir Sahib.
label: Festival
imageCaption: Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur Sahib, where the Khalsa was created

title: Bandi Chhor Divas / Diwali
summary: Bandi Chhor Divas remembers the release of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji from Gwalior Fort with fifty-two kings holding his cloak. The story and the lights of Amritsar.
body:
Bandi Chhor Divas, the Day of Liberation, falls on the same day as Diwali. Sikhs celebrate it in memory of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, who refused to leave his imprisonment in the fort of Gwalior unless fifty-two kings held with him were set free too.

## The Guru at Gwalior

Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, the sixth Guru, built Sri Akal Takht Sahib and raised a body of armed Sikhs, and the emperor Jahangir grew wary of him. On a pretext, which tradition links to an unpaid fine imposed on his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the Guru was held in the fort of Gwalior, where many princes were kept as political prisoners. Sikhs came from Punjab to bow at the walls of the fort, and the Guru's presence comforted the other prisoners.

## The cloak of fifty-two tassels

When Jahangir ordered the Guru's release, the Guru refused to go unless the fifty-two kings imprisoned with him were also freed. The emperor, thinking few could escape, said that as many as could hold on to the Guru's cloak might leave with him. The Guru had a cloak made with fifty-two tassels, and every king walked out holding one. He became known as the Bandi Chhor, the liberator of prisoners. Gurdwara Data Bandi Chhor Sahib now stands at Gwalior Fort.

## The lights of Amritsar

When the Guru reached Amritsar, the city lit lamps to welcome him. The tradition continues: on Bandi Chhor Divas, Sri Harmandir Sahib and the whole complex are lit with lamps and candles, fireworks light the sky over the sarovar, and sangats fill the parikarma. In gurdwaras and homes everywhere, Sikhs light lamps, hold kirtan and Ardas, and share sweets.
label: Festival
imageCaption: Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, lit up every year on Bandi Chhor Divas

title: Sikh New Year – Nanakshahi 559
summary: The Nanakshahi year 559 begins on 1 Chet, 14 March 2027. What the Nanakshahi calendar is, how its years are counted from 1469, and how the Sikh New Year is kept.
body:
The Sikh New Year falls on 1 Chet, the first day of the first month of the Nanakshahi calendar. On 14 March 2027 the year 559 begins. The day is also the Sangrand of Chet, the start of the new solar month.

## The Nanakshahi calendar

The Nanakshahi calendar counts its years from 1469, the year of the birth of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, so the year that runs from March 2026 to March 2027 is 558. Its twelve months carry the old Punjabi names, from Chet and Vaisakh to Magh and Phagan, the same months the Gurus used in the Barah Maha compositions of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. A version of the calendar designed by Pal Singh Purewal was adopted by the SGPC in 2003, with months of fixed length; it was later amended, and today the SGPC's calendar keeps fixed solar dates for some days and follows the moon for others, such as the Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Hazri's calendar follows the SGPC's for 558.

## The Barah Maha

Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji in Raag Tukhari and Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji in Raag Maajh each composed a Barah Maha, a song of the twelve months, in which the changing seasons mirror the longing of the soul for the Divine. Chet, the month of spring, opens both. At the Sangrand of each month, many gurdwaras recite the part of the Barah Maha for that month.

## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas, and for the recital of the Barah Maha of Chet. Many Sikhs begin the year by rising at Amrit Vela and resolving to keep their Nitnem through the year ahead. Hazri adds the calendar for each new year before it begins.
label: Festival

title: Sri Muktsar Sahib Jorh Mela – Chali Mukte
summary: The battle of Khidrana, where forty Singhs led by Mai Bhago Ji returned to fight for the Guru, and the torn disclaimer of Bhai Mahan Singh. The Maghi mela at Muktsar.
body:
Sri Muktsar Sahib remembers the battle of Khidrana in 1705, where forty Singhs who had once deserted Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji came back and gave their lives for him, and were blessed as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones. The SGPC's calendar keeps two days: a Shaheedi Divas in spring, and the great Jorh Mela on Maghi, the first day of Magh.

## The disclaimer

During the long siege of Anandpur Sahib, a group of Sikhs from the Majha, worn down by hunger, told the Guru they wished to leave. He asked them to write that they were no longer his Sikhs, and forty signed the disclaimer, the bedava, and went home. There they were met with scorn. Mai Bhago Ji, a woman of Jhabal, shamed them for leaving the Guru in his hour of need and led them back to find him, riding at their head.

## Khidrana

They caught up with the Guru in the dry Malwa near the pool of Khidrana, with a Mughal army in pursuit. Taking position at the water, the forty and Mai Bhago Ji fought off the attack while the Guru shot arrows from a nearby mound. The army withdrew, but all forty fell, and Mai Bhago Ji was wounded.

## The torn page

Walking among the fallen, the Guru found one Singh, Bhai Mahan Singh, still alive, and took his head in his lap. Bhai Mahan Singh asked him to tear up the disclaimer. The Guru took it out and tore it, and Bhai Mahan Singh died in peace. The Guru blessed the forty as the Chali Mukte, and Khidrana became Muktsar, the pool of liberation.

## The Jorh Mela

Every Maghi, vast sangats gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib to bathe in the sarovar and for kirtan, Ardas and a great Nagar Kirtan. Every Ardas remembers the forty.

title: Jorh Mela – Baba Bakala Sahib
summary: The Jorh Mela at Baba Bakala Sahib on Rakhar Puniya remembers how Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana found Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji and cried Guru ladho re. The mela and its story.
body:
The Jorh Mela at Baba Bakala Sahib, held on Rakhar Puniya, the full moon of Sawan, remembers the day in 1664 when Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana found the true Guru among many claimants at Bakala, and called out to the sangat: Guru ladho re, I have found the Guru. It is one of the largest melas of the Majha.

## Twenty-two Gurus at Bakala

Before his Joti Jot in Delhi, Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji said only that the next Guru would be found at Bakala, a town near the Beas. Twenty-two members of the Sodhi family hurried to set up seats there, each claiming the Guruship. Meanwhile, Tegh Bahadur Ji, the youngest son of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, lived quietly at Bakala in meditation, in a room below the ground, making no claim at all.

## The test of the coins

Bhai Makhan Shah, a Lubana trader, had prayed to the Guru when his ship was in a storm and vowed five hundred gold coins if he reached shore. At Bakala he put two coins before each claimant and waited. Each accepted the two and blessed him. Then he was told of one more holy man, and found Tegh Bahadur Ji, who asked why he was offering two coins when he had promised five hundred, and showed the mark on his shoulder where he had pushed the ship to safety. Makhan Shah climbed onto a roof and called the sangat to their Guru.

## The mela

Gurdwara Baba Bakala Sahib, with Gurdwara Bhora Sahib at the place of the underground room, draws sangats from across Punjab for the mela, with kirtan, katha, Ardas and langar. Read the story of the Gurgaddi of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji.
label: Jor Mela
imageCaption: Gurdwara Baba Bakala Sahib, Amritsar district

title: Jorh Mela – Kandh Sahib, Batala
summary: Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji married Mata Sulakhani Ji at Batala in 1487. The wall of Gurdwara Kandh Sahib, Gurdwara Dehra Sahib, and the Jorh Mela held in Batala every year.
body:
The Jorh Mela at Gurdwara Kandh Sahib in Batala, Gurdaspur district, remembers the marriage of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Mata Sulakhani Ji, which tradition places in 1487. It is the largest annual gathering in Batala, a celebration as much as a remembrance.

## The wedding at Batala

Mata Sulakhani Ji was the daughter of Bhai Mool Chand Chona, a Khatri of Pakhoke Randhawa, who was living at Batala. The young Nanak, then working at Sultanpur Lodhi, came to Batala with his wedding party, accompanied by his family and friends. Tradition remembers that the bride's family, being followers of old customs, were uneasy that the groom would not perform all the usual rituals, and that some of them argued with the Guru.

## The wall that did not fall

The wedding party was seated beside an old mud wall, and tradition remembers that some hoped it would fall on the Guru. An old woman warned him that the wall was about to collapse; the Guru answered calmly that it would stand for ages to come. A part of that mud wall, the kandh, is still preserved under glass at Gurdwara Kandh Sahib, which takes its name from it. Gurdwara Dehra Sahib in Batala marks the place where the wedding ceremony was held.

## Family life

Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Mata Sulakhani Ji had two sons, Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. The Guru's marriage is often recalled as part of his teaching that the spiritual life is lived within the family, not by renouncing it.

## The Jorh Mela

The mela is held each year with Nagar Kirtan recreating the wedding procession from Sultanpur Lodhi, kirtan, Ardas and langar.
label: Jor Mela
imageCaption: Gurdwara Kandh Sahib, Batala, where the mud wall is preserved

title: Chola Sahib Jorh Mela – Dera Baba Nanak
summary: Gurdwara Chola Sahib at Dera Baba Nanak keeps a cloak believed to have been given to Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji on his travels. Its story, Dera Baba Nanak, and the March mela.
body:
The Chola Sahib Jorh Mela is held each year in early March at Dera Baba Nanak, in Gurdaspur district, close to the border with Pakistan. It centres on the Chola Sahib, a cloak kept at the gurdwara of that name and believed by tradition to have been given to Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji on his travels to the west.

## The Chola Sahib

The Chola Sahib is a long cloak covered in writing in Arabic script, with verses and names in praise of the Divine. Tradition holds that it was presented to Guru Nanak Dev Ji by admirers during his udasi to the lands of Islam, often said to be at Baghdad or Mecca, as a mark of the respect in which he was held. It was kept by the Guru's descendants and later came to Dera Baba Nanak, where it is shown to the sangat at the mela. Historians have discussed its origin and its inscriptions, and sangats regard it with deep reverence.

## Dera Baba Nanak

Dera Baba Nanak stands on the Indian side of the Ravi, across the river from Kartarpur, where Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his last years. After his passing, his family settled here, and the town grew around the dera of the Guru's descendants. Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in the town is associated with the Guru's visits. Since 2019 the Kartarpur Corridor has begun here, letting pilgrims cross without a visa to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, a few kilometres away.

## The Jorh Mela

For several days the town fills with sangats for kirtan, Ardas and langar, and for the showing of the Chola Sahib. Many pilgrims also visit the viewing platform from which Kartarpur Sahib can be seen across the border.
label: Jor Mela

title: Miri-Piri Divas – Sixth Patshahi
summary: Miri-Piri Divas remembers the two swords of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, for worldly and spiritual authority, and the balance at the heart of Sikh life. The day explained.
body:
Miri-Piri Divas remembers the teaching of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, the sixth Guru, who wore two swords: one of Miri, worldly authority and responsibility, and one of Piri, spiritual authority. The day reminds Sikhs that devotion and the duty to stand up for justice belong together.

## The two swords

When Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji became Guru in 1606, after the martyrdom of his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, he put aside the seli, the woollen cord worn by the earlier Gurus, and girded himself with two swords. He built Sri Akal Takht Sahib facing Sri Harmandir Sahib, kept horses and armed Sikhs, and asked Sikhs to bring weapons as offerings. The Sikhs, who had seen their Guru tortured to death, learned to defend themselves and others.

## Saint and soldier

Tradition remembers a meeting between the Guru and Samarth Ramdas, the Maratha saint, who asked how a follower of Guru Nanak could carry weapons and ride like a king. The Guru is remembered as answering that he was a householder outwardly and a renunciate within, that the sword was to protect the poor and destroy the tyrant, and that Guru Nanak had renounced not the world but the self. The idea was carried forward by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji in the Khalsa, the saint-soldier, and the Khanda, the Sikh emblem, includes two curved swords for Miri and Piri.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras hold kirtan, katha and Ardas, especially at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, and many hold displays of gatka. It is a day to think about how faith shapes the way one acts in the world.
label: Special day
imageCaption: Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, in the 1920s

title: Sikh Dastaar Divas / World Sikh Turban Day
summary: Dastaar Divas, kept the day before Vaisakhi, celebrates the Sikh turban: why Sikhs wear it, what it means, and how turban-tying camps mark the day around the world.
body:
Sikh Dastaar Divas, also called World Sikh Turban Day, is kept on the day before Vaisakhi, when the Khalsa was created in 1699. It celebrates the dastaar, the Sikh turban, and invites people of every background to learn what it means, and sometimes to try one on.

## Why Sikhs wear the dastaar

Kes, uncut hair, is the first of the five Ks that Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji gave the Khalsa, and the dastaar covers and protects it. In the India of the Gurus' time, a turban was worn by kings and nobles, and the low castes were forbidden to wear one. The Gurus gave it to every Sikh, man or woman, as a sign that all are equal and sovereign under the Guru, and as a reminder to live up to that dignity. A Sikh's turban is treated with respect, and tying it each morning is part of the day's discipline.

## A visible faith

The dastaar makes a Sikh recognisable anywhere, which the Guru intended: a Sikh could not hide in a crowd and was expected to stand up for those in need. Sikhs have often had to defend the right to wear it, in schools, workplaces and armies, and many have been targeted because of it. Dastaar Divas grew out of efforts by Sikh organisations in the 2000s to build that understanding.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras and Sikh groups hold turban-tying camps for children and young people, competitions in tying the dastaar, and stalls in public places where anyone can have a turban tied and learn about it. In Punjab many schools and colleges take part.
label: Special day
imageCaption: The dastaar, worn by Sikhs as a crown of faith

title: India Independence Day
summary: Why the SGPC's calendar marks 15 August: the part Sikhs played in India's freedom struggle, from the Kukas and the Ghadar Party to Jallianwala Bagh and the Akali morchas.
body:
India became independent on 15 August 1947, and the SGPC's calendar marks the day. For Sikhs, it is a day to remember the very large part their community played in the freedom struggle, and also, because independence came with the Partition of Punjab, a day of mixed memory.

## A share far beyond their numbers

Sikhs were less than two percent of India's people, yet they were heavily represented among those hanged, imprisoned and transported for the freedom struggle. The Kuka or Namdhari movement under Baba Ram Singh resisted British rule from the 1860s, and many Kukas were blown from cannon at Malerkotla in 1872. The Ghadar Party, founded in 1913 by Indians on the Pacific coast of America, most of them Punjabi Sikhs, sent hundreds home to raise a revolt; Kartar Singh Sarabha and many others were hanged. Bhagat Singh came from a Sikh family steeped in the struggle.

## Jallianwala Bagh and the morchas

The massacre at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on Vaisakhi in 1919, where hundreds were killed, many of them pilgrims, turned much of India against British rule. The non-violent morchas of the Gurdwara Reform Movement in the early 1920s, at Guru Ka Bagh, Jaito and over the keys of the Toshakhana, were among the first mass campaigns to force the government's hand. Sikh soldiers in the Indian National Army, and leaders such as Baba Kharak Singh and Master Tara Singh, also played their part.

## How the day is observed

Many gurdwaras hold Ardas for those who gave their lives for freedom. The next day, the SGPC's calendar remembers the people of Punjab killed in the Partition. Read about the Partition Ardas day.
label: Special day

title: Ardas Day for Punjabis killed during the 1947 Partition
summary: The day after Independence, the SGPC's calendar remembers the Punjabis of every faith killed in the Partition of 1947, and the Sikh shrines left behind in Pakistan.
body:
On the day after India's Independence, the SGPC's calendar keeps an Ardas Day for the Punjabis who were killed during the Partition of 1947. It remembers the people of Punjab, Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims alike, who lost their lives, their homes and their land when the province was divided between India and Pakistan.

## A divided Punjab

The new border, announced only after independence, ran through the heart of Punjab. Lahore, the capital of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, went to Pakistan, and so did Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Kartarpur, where he spent his last years, Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore, Panja Sahib, and hundreds of other places sacred to the Sikhs, along with much of the fertile canal land that Sikh farmers had settled.

## The killing and the migration

In the months around August 1947 Punjab was swept by communal violence. Trains arrived full of the dead, villages were burned, and women were abducted or killed, some by their own families to save them from capture. Estimates of the dead across the subcontinent run from several hundred thousand to two million, and Punjab bore the greatest share. Some ten million people crossed the new border in one of the largest migrations in history. Nearly every Sikh family from West Punjab carries stories of what was lost.

## The daily Ardas

Since 1947 the Sikh Ardas has included a prayer for free access to, and care of, the gurdwaras and shrines from which the Panth has been separated. The opening of the Kartarpur Corridor in 2019 answered part of that prayer.

## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras hold Ardas for all those killed, and many families remember the villages and homes their parents and grandparents left behind.
label: Special day

title: Punjabi Suba Day
summary: On 1 November 1966 Punjab was reorganised as a Punjabi-speaking state after the long Punjabi Suba movement. The movement, its leaders, and what was left unsettled.
body:
Punjabi Suba Day marks 1 November 1966, when the state of Punjab was reorganised on the basis of language, creating a Punjabi-speaking state. It was the result of the Punjabi Suba movement, one of the longest political campaigns in the history of the state, in which Sikhs played the leading part.

## States by language

After independence, India began to redraw its states along the lines of language, and in 1956 many new linguistic states were formed. The demand for a Punjabi-speaking state, where Punjabi in the Gurmukhi script would be the language of government and schooling, was set aside. The Shiromani Akali Dal, under Master Tara Singh and later Sant Fateh Singh, led the campaign for it.

## The movement

Through the 1950s and 1960s, tens of thousands of volunteers courted arrest in morchas, and in 1955 police entered the complex of Sri Harmandir Sahib to arrest protesters. Leaders went on fasts unto death. After the war of 1965, in which Punjab and its soldiers bore much of the burden, the central government agreed to reorganise the state.

## The reorganisation of 1966

On 1 November 1966 the old Punjab was divided: the Hindi-speaking south became Haryana, the hill districts went to Himachal Pradesh, and Chandigarh, the capital, was made a union territory shared by Punjab and Haryana. The questions of Chandigarh, of Punjabi-speaking areas left outside the state, and of river waters remained unsettled, and came back in the demands of later years.

## How the day is observed

The day is marked with events celebrating Punjabi language and culture, and in some gurdwaras with Ardas for those who took part in the movement.
label: Special day

title: Foundation Day – SGPC
summary: The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee was formed at Sri Akal Takht Sahib on 15 November 1920 to free the gurdwaras from the mahants. Its history and its work today.
body:
The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, the SGPC, was founded on 15 November 1920 at a gathering at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. It was formed to bring the historic gurdwaras of the Sikhs under the management of the Panth itself, and today it manages Sri Harmandir Sahib and many other gurdwaras.

## The gurdwaras under the mahants

In the nineteenth century, many historic gurdwaras had passed into the hands of hereditary mahants, who ran them as private property and often allowed practices contrary to the Gurus' teaching. Sri Harmandir Sahib itself was run by a manager appointed by the British government. Early in the twentieth century, the Singh Sabha movement had revived Sikh learning and identity, and a demand grew for the Panth to manage its own shrines.

## A committee of the Panth

In October 1920 a group of Sikhs from castes the priests treated as low came to Sri Harmandir Sahib with an offering, which the priests refused. The sangat took a hukam from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, which welcomed them; the priests fled, and the Sikhs took charge of Sri Akal Takht Sahib. A month later, a large gathering formed a committee of 175 members to manage the gurdwaras, the SGPC. Within weeks the Shiromani Akali Dal was formed to organise volunteers.

## The reform movement

The years that followed saw the morchas at Nankana Sahib, Guru Ka Bagh, Jaito and over the keys of the Toshakhana. The movement ended with the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925, which gave the SGPC legal charge of the historic gurdwaras of Punjab, with its members elected by Sikh voters.

## Its work today

The SGPC manages gurdwaras, runs schools, colleges and hospitals, publishes Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and sets the Nanakshahi calendar that Hazri follows.
label: Special day

title: Foundation Day – Shiromani Akali Dal
summary: The Shiromani Akali Dal was founded on 14 December 1920 to organise volunteers for the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Its origins in the morchas and its later history.
body:
The Shiromani Akali Dal was founded on 14 December 1920, a month after the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. The SGPC's calendar keeps its foundation day because of the place the Akali Dal held in the Gurdwara Reform Movement, the struggle to bring the historic gurdwaras into the Panth's own hands.

## The Akali jathas

The word akali means a follower of the Timeless One, Akal, and recalls the Akali Nihangs of the eighteenth century, who served the Panth and guarded its shrines. In 1920, as Sikhs began to take over gurdwaras from the mahants, local bands of volunteers called Akali jathas formed across Punjab. The Shiromani Akali Dal was created to coordinate them as a central body, with Sardar Sarmukh Singh Jhabal as its first president.

## The morchas

Akali volunteers carried the weight of the reform movement. They faced the massacre at Nankana Sahib in 1921, the beatings at Guru Ka Bagh in 1922, and the firing at Jaito in 1924, keeping to their pledge of non-violence. Their sacrifices led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 and earned the respect of the national movement.

## A political party

After 1925 the Akali Dal became the main political voice of the Sikhs. It led the Punjabi Suba movement, which created the Punjabi-speaking state in 1966, opposed the Emergency of 1975, and led the Dharam Yudh Morcha of the 1980s. It has formed governments in Punjab several times. Today there are several groups claiming the Akali name, and views of the party's record differ, as with any political body.

## How the day is observed

The day is marked with Ardas and gatherings, especially at Sri Akal Takht Sahib.
label: Special day

title: Sangrand
summary: What Sangrand is, why Sikhs gather at the gurdwara on the first day of each month to hear the Barah Maha, and every Sangrand date of Nanakshahi 558.
body:
Sangrand is the first day of each month of the Nanakshahi calendar, the day on which the sun enters a new sign of the zodiac. The name comes from the Sanskrit sankranti, a passing over. There are twelve Sangrands in the year, and on each one many Sikhs go to the gurdwara in the morning to begin the new month in the Guru's presence.

## The Barah Maha

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji holds two compositions called Barah Maha, songs of the twelve months: one by Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji in Raag Tukhari and one by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji in Raag Maajh. Each month's verses describe the season, the heat of Jeth, the rains of Sawan, the cold of Poh, and use it to speak of the soul's longing for the Divine. On Sangrand, gurdwaras read the verses for the new month, and the granthi announces the name of the month to the sangat.

## A Sikh view of the day

In the older Indian tradition, sankranti days were thought auspicious or inauspicious, and people bathed in holy rivers or gave alms to ward off ill fortune. The Gurus taught that no day is lucky or unlucky in itself, and that a day is blessed when the Divine is remembered in it. Sikhs keep Sangrand not as a ritual but as an occasion to listen to the Barah Maha and begin the month with Ardas. Some Sikh scholars discourage giving it special weight at all, and every day is equally the Guru's.

## How Sangrand is observed

Gurdwaras hold a morning programme of kirtan, the reading of the Barah Maha, katha and Ardas, followed by langar. Two Sangrands are also festivals: the Sangrand of Vaisakh is Vaisakhi, and the Sangrand of Magh is Maghi, the Jorh Mela at Sri Muktsar Sahib. The Sangrand of Chet is the Sikh New Year. Hazri shows every Sangrand in its calendar.

title: Masya
summary: What Masya, the new moon day, means in Sikh practice, why sangats gather at Tarn Taran Sahib and other gurdwaras, and every Masya date of Nanakshahi 558.
body:
Masya is the day of the new moon, when the moon cannot be seen, and it comes once in every lunar month, about every twenty-nine and a half days. In the Nanakshahi calendar for 558 there are twelve. In Punjab it is a day when large sangats gather at certain historic gurdwaras.

## Masya in Punjab

In Indian tradition the new moon, amavas, was long kept as a day for bathing in sacred waters, remembering ancestors and giving alms. Sikh tradition has kept the gathering but changed its meaning. On Masya, sangats travel to gurdwaras associated with the Gurus to hear kirtan and to bathe in the sarovar, and the best known of these gatherings is at Sri Darbar Sahib, Tarn Taran, the town founded by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, whose sarovar is among the largest of all. Gurdwaras at Goindwal Sahib, Khadur Sahib, Baba Bakala and many other places also draw great numbers. At Sri Muktsar Sahib and Chheharta Sahib, a monthly Masya mela is a long tradition.

## What the Gurus taught

The Gurus taught that bathing at a holy place does not wash away the dirt of the mind, and that the true pilgrimage is to bathe in the Name. Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji questioned those who thought a dip at a particular moment could earn merit. Sikhs who keep Masya do so as a day to be in the sangat and to remember the Divine, not out of belief that the new moon itself is holy.

## How Masya is observed

Gurdwaras that keep the day hold kirtan from early morning, katha and Ardas, and serve langar to the large sangats. Many families make Masya their monthly visit to a historic gurdwara near them. Hazri lists every Masya in its calendar.

title: Puranmashi
summary: What Puranmashi, the full moon, means for Sikhs: the Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, monthly gatherings and Sukhmani Sahib, and every full moon date of Nanakshahi 558.
body:
Puranmashi is the day of the full moon, which comes once in every lunar month. In the Nanakshahi calendar for 558 there are eleven, from April 2026 to February 2027. For many Sikhs it is a day to gather in the sangat, and one full moon in particular is the most celebrated day of the Sikh year.

## The full moon of Katak

The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Nanak Gurpurab, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Katak, which is why its date moves each year. On that night, gurdwaras are lit, and many Sikhs keep a vigil of kirtan into the night. Several other days are also tied to the full moon in Sikh tradition, among them Rakhar Puniya, the full moon of Sawan, when the Jorh Mela at Baba Bakala Sahib is held. Read about Guru Nanak Dev Ji's Prakash Purab.

## Puranmashi in the gurdwara

Many gurdwaras, especially in villages and towns of Punjab, hold a special programme every Puranmashi, often a Sukhmani Sahib paath, kirtan and Ardas in the evening, with langar. Some sangats complete a Sahaj Paath or an Akhand Paath each month on the full moon. In the old Punjab the full moon gave light for travel at night, and the custom of gathering on Puranmashi may have grown from that.

## What the Gurus taught

As with Sangrand and Masya, the Gurus taught that no day is holy in itself, and that what makes any day blessed is remembering the Divine. Sikhs who keep Puranmashi keep it as a time for the sangat.

## How Puranmashi is observed

Gurdwaras hold kirtan, Sukhmani Sahib, katha and Ardas. Hazri shows every Puranmashi in its calendar.
